clause: 210.3(b) definitions (Part 210; adopted into Part 211 by 211.3 but not in the uploaded files)
requirement: Part 210 definitions, which Part 211 adopts through 211.3: a lot, control or batch number is any unique code of letters, digits or symbols from which the full manufacturing, processing, packing, holding and distribution history of a batch or lot can be reconstructed. Theoretical yield is what a phase would produce from the components used if nothing were lost and no error occurred; actual yield is what the phase really produces; percentage of theoretical yield is actual divided by theoretical for the same phase, expressed as a percent. (Could not be checked here: Part 210 is not among the uploaded texts.)
system_implications: (1) Lot numbers must be unique per site+material (enforced by a uniqueness constraint) and carry a globally unique internal key so multi-site genealogy never collides. (2) Every lot number must resolve to its complete history: effective MBR version, executed BPR, every step/signature, every component and intermediate lot consumed, equipment and rooms used, IPC/QC results, deviations/investigations, packaging, serialization, disposition, and distribution shipments. (3) Genealogy must support backward (finished lot -> all inputs, any depth) and forward (component lot -> all intermediates, finished lots, shipments) traversal, including splits, merges, rework/reprocessing and inter-site transfers. This definition is the main regulatory driver for a graph-shaped genealogy model (see US-GEN-01). (4) Yield formulas per phase are defined in the MBR (numerator, denominator, units, rounding) and computed by the system; users cannot type a yield percentage (a design choice: 211.103 would also allow a manual calculation checked by a second person). Even when the system calculates the yield, 211.103 still requires one person to verify it independently, so a verifier sign-off is mandatory. Scope notes: serialization links come from DSCSA, not Part 210/211; room-level history is good practice rather than a stated element.
note: Part 210 is not in the uploaded files; 211.3 only incorporates 210.3 by reference, so these definitions could not be checked against official text here. Requirement reworded only to avoid transcription; substance unchanged. Closest anchors in the uploaded Part 211: 211.130(c) (lot number must let the batch's manufacturing and control history be determined), 211.103, 211.186(b)(7) and 211.188(b)(7) (yields). Implication (4) fell short: automated yield still needs independent verification by one person under 211.103.

requirement: A quality control unit (QCU) must exist with the responsibility and authority to approve or reject every component, drug product container, closure, in-process material, packaging material, labeling item and drug product, and to review production records to make sure no errors occurred or that any errors were fully investigated. The QCU also approves or rejects products that another company makes, processes, packs or holds for the firm under contract. The QCU approves or rejects every procedure or specification that affects identity, strength, quality or purity. QCU responsibilities and procedures must be written down and followed. (211.22(b), laboratory facilities available to the QCU, is not an eBMR function.)
system_implications: Material and batch disposition (Released, Rejected, Quarantine) is a Quality-only permission. A 'conditional release' status, if the SOP defines one, may only permit movement under quarantine (e.g., to another site for packaging or testing); it must never enable distribution before the 211.165(a) testing and the 211.192 record review are complete. Production roles can never change the status of any material, intermediate or batch. MBR/recipe/specification activation requires a QA approval e-signature. Segregation of duties is enforced by default (good practice supporting QCU independence, not explicit 211.22 text): a user who executed or verified steps on a batch cannot sign QA disposition for that batch. Disposition is an e-signature with an explicit meaning ('Approved for release' / 'Rejected'). Status is a single source of truth consumed by dispensing, packaging and shipping, which all apply hard stops against it. Added: for batches made by a contract manufacturer, the eBMR must hold (or receive) the contracting firm's QCU approve/reject decision, and a CMO-side release must not be treated as the owner's disposition. In-process materials, packaging materials and labeling also carry QCU-controlled statuses, not only batches and components.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Added the omitted sentence of 211.22(a) on QCU approval of contract-manufactured products. Implications: open-ended 'conditional release' could conflict with 211.165(a)/211.192, so it is limited to quarantine movements; segregation of QA disposition from execution flagged as good practice beyond the text; contract-manufacturing disposition added.

requirement: Everyone who manufactures, processes, packs or holds a drug product needs education, training and experience (any combination is acceptable) sufficient for the assigned functions. Training must cover the specific operations the person performs and CGMP as it applies to their job, including the CGMP regulations and the SOPs they require; CGMP training is delivered by qualified people, continually and often enough that staff stay familiar with the requirements that apply to them. Supervisors need qualifications that let them supervise in a way that assures the product's safety, identity, strength, quality and purity, and there must be enough qualified staff to perform and supervise each product's operations.
system_implications: Before a user can execute, verify, review or approve an MBR step, the system checks that the user holds a current qualification for that operation, SOP version, equipment and MBR (through an LMS integration or an internal curriculum). A missing or expired qualification is a hard stop that names the missing item. A supervisor cannot sign on the user's behalf and there is no override. The system stores a snapshot of the qualification evidence (curriculum item, version, completion date) with each executed signature. Aseptic edition: the user must also hold a current gowning qualification and have taken part in a successful aseptic process simulation (media fill) for the line/role. Scope notes: the hard-stop qualification check, the no-override rule and the qualification snapshot are good-practice design choices (211.25 requires trained staff but does not prescribe system gating). The aseptic gowning qualification and media-fill participation rules come from FDA's 2004 aseptic processing guidance, not from 211.25. For users of the eBMR itself, 11.10(i) adds that people who develop, maintain or use the system must be trained for those tasks.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Minor wording fix: the rule accepts any combination of education, training and experience, not necessarily all three. Implications kept; flagged which controls are good practice or guidance-derived (aseptic gowning, APS participation) rather than regulatory text.

requirement: Staff wear clean clothing suited to their duties, plus protective apparel (head, face, hand and arm coverings) as needed to protect product from contamination, and practise good sanitation and health habits. Only people authorized by supervisors may enter areas designated as limited-access. Anyone who appears ill or has open lesions that could harm product safety or quality (whether a medical exam or a supervisor noticed it) is kept away from direct contact with components, containers, closures, in-process materials and product until the condition is corrected or competent medical staff clear them; all staff are told to report such health conditions to supervisors.
system_implications: Injectables: the eBMR records, or imports from access control, who entered Grade A/B (ISO 5/7) areas during the batch and when. Only persons with a current gowning qualification can be assigned to aseptic steps. This personnel-presence list is part of the batch record and supports EM excursion investigations. Tablets: area access authorization is checked for restricted rooms such as potent compound suites (configurable). Scope notes: 211.28 does not require the batch record to list who entered classified areas, nor gowning-qualification gating; the Grade A/B and ISO 5/7 terms and gowning qualification come from EU Annex 1 and FDA's 2004 aseptic guidance, so keep them as good practice. What 211.28(c) does require is supervisor-authorized entry to limited-access areas, so step execution in such an area should be limited to users on the authorized list (from the eBMR or the access-control system it reads). Optional: a fitness-for-duty attestation at aseptic-area sign-in to support 211.28(d).
note: Clause correct; paraphrase was faithful but omitted (b) hygiene habits and the duty in (d) to report health conditions, now added. Implications flagged as guidance-derived (personnel presence list, gowning qualification) and tied back to the actual 211.28(c) authorization requirement.

requirement: Aseptic processing areas must include, as appropriate: smooth, hard, easily cleaned floors, walls and ceilings; temperature and humidity control; HEPA-filtered supply air at positive pressure, whether or not the airflow is laminar; a system to monitor environmental conditions; a system to clean and disinfect the room and equipment so aseptic conditions are achieved; and a system to maintain the equipment that controls aseptic conditions. These are facility requirements; the eBMR's role is to check and record their status for the batch.
system_implications: The eBMR must record, or interface to: room/zone cleaning and disinfection status (agent, lot, contact time, performer, clean-hold expiry); differential pressure, temperature and RH within limits during the batch window (from BMS/EMS); and execution of the batch-specific EM sampling plan (viable air, surfaces, settle plates, personnel glove/gown), with results linked to the batch when available. Any EMS/BMS alarm during the batch time window is attached to the batch automatically for review. The aseptic filling step cannot start unless the room/line status is 'Released for aseptic operation'. Scope notes: 211.42(c)(10) requires these systems to exist; it does not itself require a batch-specific EM sampling plan, automatic alarm attachment or a 'released for aseptic operation' gate. Those come from FDA's 2004 aseptic processing guidance (EM data reviewed as part of batch release), and blocking release for missing EM results rests on 211.192 once the firm defines EM records as part of the batch's control records. Keep them as good practice and state that basis in the URS.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; added the 'as appropriate' qualifier. Implications go beyond the literal text (batch EM plan, alarm linkage, room-status gate); kept as guidance-based good practice and labelled as such.

requirement: Equipment must be suitably designed, large enough and placed so that it supports its intended operations and its cleaning and maintenance. Equipment and utensils are cleaned and maintained, and sanitized and/or sterilized where the drug requires it, at intervals that prevent malfunction or contamination that would push product quality outside established requirements. Written, followed procedures must cover: who is responsible; cleaning, maintenance and (where needed) sanitizing schedules; enough detail on methods, equipment and materials, including dismantling and reassembly; removing or obliterating the previous batch's identification; protecting clean equipment until use; and checking equipment is clean immediately before use. Cleaning, maintenance, sanitizing and inspection are recorded as 211.180 and 211.182 require.
system_implications: The equipment master has a state machine (Dirty, Cleaning, Clean, In Use, Maintenance, Out of Service, Calibration Due) with configurable clean-hold and dirty-hold time limits and campaign rules. At step start the operator scans the equipment ID and the system checks: state = Clean, clean-hold time not expired, allowed for this product (dedicated/campaign/product-change cleaning level), and preventive maintenance and calibration current. A pre-use cleanliness inspection e-signature is mandatory and recorded in the BPR. At release from use, the equipment becomes Dirty and the dirty-hold timer starts. Cleaning runs from an electronic cleaning record (method version, agents, performer, verifier) that removes the previous batch identification (status label reprint). Scope notes: clean-hold and dirty-hold limits and campaign rules are not stated in 211.67; they are validation-derived good practice implementing 211.67(a) and (b)(5). Recording the pre-use inspection inside the BPR is good practice; the rule allows it in the equipment log (211.182), except that for dedicated equipment the cleaning, maintenance and use records must be part of the batch record. Added for 211.63: the MBR should name the permitted equipment class and capacity per step so unsuitable equipment is rejected at scan.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications: hold-time rules labelled as validation-derived good practice; added an equipment-suitability check for 211.63, which the original did not address.

requirement: Automatic, mechanical or electronic equipment, including computers and related systems, may be used in manufacturing, processing, packing and holding if it performs its function satisfactorily. When it is used, it must be routinely calibrated, inspected or checked under a written program designed to assure proper performance, and written records of those calibration checks and inspections must be kept.
system_implications: The instrument/scale master holds calibration due dates and any required daily or pre-use checks (for example, balance check weights with acceptance tolerance). Using an instrument whose calibration is overdue, or whose daily check is missing or failed, is a hard stop. The BPR records instrument ID, calibration due date and check result for every measurement. Weights come directly from the balance interface (gross/tare/net, unit, balance ID, timestamp, raw device string). Manual keying is only allowed in a documented fallback mode, which triggers two-person verification (see US-211-68C). Scope notes: daily/pre-use checks, storage of raw device strings and per-measurement recording of calibration due dates are good-practice choices beyond 211.68(a). The hard stop on overdue or failed instruments is consistent with 211.160(b)(4), which bars use of instruments that do not meet their specifications. Added: 211.68(a) also covers the eBMR itself as a computer or related system, so the platform needs a documented routine check program (e.g., periodic review, interface and backup checks, time-sync checks) with records.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct (the rule is permissive: such equipment may be used, but must then be checked under a written program). Implications: flagged good-practice items; added that the eBMR platform itself falls under the routine-check program.

requirement: Computer or related systems must be controlled so that only authorized personnel can change master production and control records or other records. Formulas and other records or data entered into and produced by the system must be checked for accuracy, with the depth and frequency of checking based on the system's complexity and reliability. A backup file of entered data must be kept, except where computerization eliminates certain data (for example laboratory calculations), in which case a written record of the program is kept with validation data. Hard-copy or alternative backups must keep the backup data exact, complete and protected against alteration, accidental erasure or loss.
system_implications: RBAC plus a versioned change-control workflow for MBRs and GMP master data (materials, specs, limits, equipment, label data); no direct database edits. Every interface (ERP, LIMS, WMS, scales, PLC/SCADA/historian, serialization L3/L4, label printers, vision systems) is validated with input/output accuracy checks: schema validation, message acknowledgment, checksums/hashes, idempotency keys, reconciliation reports, and a dead-letter queue that raises alarms. Calculations run in a versioned, validated formula engine, and the formula version is stored with each result. Backups are automated, encrypted, immutable (WORM/object-lock) true copies that include metadata, audit trails and signatures. They are retained for the full records-retention period, and restore tests run periodically. These are separate from transient disaster-recovery snapshots (per the FDA DI Q&A definition of backup). Scope notes: 211.68(b) scales input/output verification to the system's complexity and reliability, so checksum and idempotency controls on every interface are a risk-based design choice rather than a mandate. WORM storage, encryption and retention of backups for the full record period follow the FDA 2018 data integrity Q&A definition of backup (guidance), not the rule text. Serialization (L3/L4) interfaces are DSCSA-driven.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications kept; noted which items are risk-based design or guidance-derived.

requirement: For the operations covered by 211.101(c) and (d) (dispensing checks and addition of components), 211.103 (yield calculation), 211.182 (equipment cleaning and maintenance log) and 211.188(b)(11) (people performing and checking significant steps), automated equipment can satisfy the requirement that one person performs and another checks, provided the equipment is used in conformity with 211.68 and one person checks that it performed the operation properly. (The statement that the 2008 rule codified a long-standing FDA view is preamble commentary and cannot be verified from the uploaded text; the eCFR source notes do confirm 211.68 was amended in September 2008.)
system_implications: Each MBR step carries a configuration flag, 'automated performance eligible' (for example: validated barcode + scale + status check for dispensing, automated yield calculation, automated CIP/SIP). In automated mode the system stores the device ID and raw data and requires one human verification e-signature with the meaning 'Verified automated operation'. If automation is unavailable (device offline, manual keying, barcode override), the system automatically escalates to two-person mode (performer + independent verifier), and the fallback is flagged in review-by-exception. The verifier in automated mode must still be a qualified person with the verification permission. Correction (falls short): the 'automated performance eligible' flag must be restricted to steps that fall under 211.101(c)/(d), 211.103, 211.182 and 211.188(b)(11). It must not relax two-person rules elsewhere, e.g., the independent check of the master record (211.186(a)), the second-person verification of 100% visual checks of hand-applied labeling (211.122(g)(3)) or the second-person review of laboratory records (211.194(a)(8)). Because the equipment must be used in conformity with 211.68, one-person mode should also require the device to be current in its calibration/check program (211.68(a)) and the automated function to be validated (211.68(b)).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; historical claim about the 2008 rule is outside the uploaded text. Implications fell short: they did not limit one-person mode to the four listed operation types or tie it to the device being current in its 211.68 program.

requirement: There must be written production and process control procedures designed to assure the product has the identity, strength, quality and purity it claims, covering every requirement of Subpart F. These procedures, and any changes, are written, reviewed and approved by the relevant organizational units and then reviewed and approved by the QCU. They must be followed when production and process control functions are carried out, and documented at the time each is performed; any departure from them must be recorded and justified.
system_implications: Contemporaneous capture: every entry is time-stamped by the server from a trusted, NTP-synchronized source, and users can never type or edit the execution timestamp. Each entry is committed durably when submitted (see US-DI-07). A 'late entry' is allowed only with a mandatory reason, stores both actual event time (if known) and entry time, and is flagged for QA. Step sequence is enforced (11.10(f)). Any departure from the MBR (out-of-range parameter, skipped/added step, material or equipment substitution, time-limit breach, instruction not followed) forces a deviation/event record with justification, linked to the QMS, before the step can be completed or the batch progress. A batch cannot move to Released until every deviation or investigation affecting it has a QCU-approved conclusion on batch impact (211.192, 211.22(a)); only follow-up actions such as CAPA may remain open, and an SOP cannot waive the impact conclusion. Scope notes: server timestamps, late-entry handling and step-sequence enforcement are implementation choices that serve the 'documented at the time of performance' requirement and 11.10(e)/(f). The cross-reference US-DI-07 points to a requirement that is not in this set.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications: the SOP-based exception allowing release with open deviations was too loose relative to 211.192 and 211.22(a); narrowed to open follow-up actions only.

requirement: Production and control procedures must make sure each batch is formulated with the intent of delivering at least 100% of the labeled or established amount of active ingredient.
system_implications: The MBR supports potency-adjusted dispensing: target API quantity = label claim x batch size / (assay of the specific QC-released lot, corrected as defined, e.g. as-is vs anhydrous/LOD/salt factor), taken from released LIMS/CoA data rather than typed in. Overages are allowed only when declared and justified in the MPCR (211.186(b)(5)). Compensating excipient adjustment (e.g., filler q.s.) is calculated by the formula engine. The system rejects any MBR or dispensing target that would yield less than 100% of label claim. Injectables: q.s. to final volume/weight with density handling. Scope note: potency-adjusted dispensing and automatic filler compensation are one way to meet the 'intent' requirement, not a mandate. The regulatory requirement is that the approved formula and dispensing targets are designed to deliver at least 100% of label claim, with any calculated excess stated in the master record (211.186(b)(5)) and any variations justified there (211.186(b)(4)).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications acceptable; potency adjustment labelled as an implementation choice.

requirement: Procedures must require components to be weighed, measured or subdivided as appropriate. When a component is transferred out of its original container, the new container must be labeled with the component name or item code, the receiving or control number, the weight or measure it holds, and the batch it was dispensed for (product name, strength and lot number).
system_implications: The system auto-prints dispensing labels containing all four data elements plus a unique container ID barcode, built only from system data (no free text). Reprints need a reason, are audit-trailed and mark the earlier label as void. The container ID becomes the key for charge-in verification and genealogy edges (component lot -> dispensed container -> batch step). Scope note: the unique container barcode, the no-free-text rule and reprint control are good practice beyond the four mandatory label data elements.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications kept; container barcode and reprint controls labelled as good practice.

requirement: Weighing, measuring or subdividing of components must be adequately supervised. A second person must examine each container dispensed to manufacturing to confirm that the QCU released the component, that the weight or measure matches the batch production record, and that the containers are properly identified. If automated equipment under 211.68 does the weighing, measuring or subdividing, one person is enough to confirm these three points.
system_implications: Hard stops: material status must be Released and within its retest/expiry date (211.84/211.87); quarantined, rejected, expired or retest-due lots cannot be dispensed. The captured weight must fall within the MBR tolerance. Container identity is checked by scan. The verifier e-signature must come from a different natural person than the performer; the system compares identities across all sessions and blocks a verifier who performed any part of the same dispense. With validated automation, one verifier is enough (US-211-68C). The dispensing record stores both identities, the timestamps and the three verification outcomes. Scope note: 211.101(c) requires QCU release; a date-based retest/expiry block is good practice implementing 211.87 (retest when needed, e.g., after long storage or adverse exposure), not a stated date rule.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications kept; retest-date blocking labelled as good practice.

requirement: One person charges each component into the batch and a different person confirms the addition; if automated equipment under 211.68 performs the charge, a single person's verification is enough.
system_implications: The charge-in step requires scanning every dispensed container (container ID must match this batch, step and material) in the order and at the process point set by the MBR. The step cannot complete while any required container is missing, and extra or unplanned containers are rejected. A performer signature and a verifier signature from two different users are required (one verifier if automated). Policy option (recommended; not specified by regulation): the verifier must sign within a configurable time window of the addition, from a terminal registered to that room, to support contemporaneous witnessing.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; the original already labels the time-window/terminal rule as a non-regulatory policy option.

requirement: At the close of every relevant stage of manufacturing, processing, packaging or holding, the actual yield and the percentage of theoretical yield must be worked out. One person does the calculation and a second person verifies it independently; if automated equipment under 211.68 calculates the yield, one person verifies it independently.
system_implications: The MBR defines yield checkpoints with a theoretical-yield basis and min/max % limits (211.186(b)(7)). Tablets: dispensed vs granulate, dried granulate, final blend, cores, coated tablets, packaged units. Injectables: compounded volume/weight, filtered bulk, units filled, units accepted after 100% inspection, units labeled/packed. The system calculates each yield (automated) and requires one independent verifier who did not enter the underlying quantities. A result outside the limits automatically creates a discrepancy/investigation (211.192) and blocks release. Manual override of a calculated yield is impossible, and correcting an underlying quantity recalculates the yield with an audit trail. Scope note: excluding the person who entered the underlying quantities from verifying, and forbidding manual override, are design choices beyond 211.103 (which only requires independent verification by one person for an automated calculation). Example checkpoints such as units accepted after 100% visual inspection are MBR configuration, not Part 211 requirements.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications consistent with the rule; design choices that go beyond it are flagged.

requirement: Every compounding or storage container, processing line and item of major equipment used for a batch must be properly marked at all times to show what it contains and, where needed, the processing phase. Major equipment carries a distinctive identification number or code, which is recorded in the batch production record so the exact equipment used for each batch is known; where a facility has only one item of a given type, its name can serve instead.
system_implications: Every major equipment unit, vessel, IBC, tank and line has a unique ID with a barcode/RFID. Each step records the specific unit ID, not just the equipment class, validated against the classes/units the MBR allows. The system prints or displays equipment status labels (product, lot, phase, status) and updates them on each state change. Portable containers (IBCs, bins, tanks) are tracked as genealogy nodes (lot -> container -> step). Scope note: barcode/RFID tagging of all containers is good practice; the rule only requires identification of contents and phase, and recording of major equipment IDs in the BPR.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: To assure batch uniformity and integrity, written procedures, established and followed, must describe the in-process controls, tests or examinations performed on suitable samples of in-process material from each batch. These controls monitor output and validate the performance of processes that could cause variability in the in-process material or the finished product. Where appropriate they include, among others: tablet or capsule weight variation, disintegration time, adequacy of mixing (uniformity and homogeneity), dissolution time and rate, clarity, completeness or pH of solutions, and bioburden testing. In-process specifications must be consistent with final product specifications and, where possible, derived from historical acceptable process averages and variability using suitable statistics; sample testing must assure conformance. The QCU approves or rejects in-process materials during production based on identity, strength, quality and purity testing as appropriate (for example when a significant phase starts or ends, or after long storage). Rejected in-process materials are identified and held under a quarantine system that prevents their use.
system_implications: The MBR defines an IPC plan: test, trigger (time-based, count-based or event-based), sample size, limits (alert/action/specification), instrument, and reaction rules. The eBMR schedules IPCs with countdown timers and escalates missed checks. Direct instrument capture (checkweigher, hardness/thickness tester, disintegration tester, pH meter, in-line NIR) is preferred. All individual values are stored, not just the mean. Out-of-limit results trigger an immediate alert, the MBR-defined reaction (adjust/hold/segregate the affected portion) and a deviation. Intermediates and bulk carry a QCU disposition status (Quarantine -> Approved/Rejected by QA e-signature) that gates the next phase when the MBR requires it, and rejected in-process material is status-blocked. Tablets: weight variation, thickness, hardness, friability, disintegration, blend uniformity/stratified sampling, LOD. Injectables: pH, appearance/clarity, density, pre-filtration bioburden, fill weight/volume checks, stopper/seal checks. Scope notes: the listed tests apply only where appropriate to the dosage form (e.g., weight variation and disintegration for tablets; clarity, pH and pre-filtration bioburden for solutions). Alert/action limits and countdown scheduling are good practice. Because 211.110(c) requires QCU approval or rejection of in-process materials as appropriate, the MBR should state at which phase points QA disposition is required rather than leaving it to per-batch choice.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; restored the 'where appropriate' qualifier on the example controls and the (b) statement that testing must assure conformance. Implications consistent; clarified where QCU in-process disposition is configured.

clause: FDA draft guidance 'Considerations for Complying With 21 CFR 211.110' (January 2025) - not in the uploaded texts
requirement: FDA's nonbinding draft thinking: in-process sampling and testing may rely on in-line, at-line and on-line measurements and on process models, including for advanced manufacturing such as continuous manufacturing or 3D printing; because a process model cannot guarantee that its assumptions stay valid at all times (for example during unplanned disturbances), a control strategy that relies on a model alone is not considered enough to satisfy 211.110. Per the original search the draft was not yet final (status not re-checked here).
system_implications: The IPC data model must support PAT and soft-sensor results as first-class in-process records: instrument/model ID and version, model diagnostics/validity status, raw spectra or inputs, sampling interface location, timestamps, and a link to material genealogy (time-based segments for continuous processes). The system must provide a confirmatory path (physical or at-line test) when a model is outside its validity domain, and must never accept a model output as the only basis for in-process acceptance. Model versions are controlled master data under change control. For continuous manufacturing, lot definition is time/quantity based (210.3 'lot') and diversion events must be recorded against the affected time segments. Scope note: the uploaded 211.110 text is technology-neutral and does not mention PAT or process models; the rule that a model output is never the sole basis for acceptance reflects the draft guidance and should be treated as good practice pending finalization. The 'lot' reference relies on Part 210, which is also outside the uploaded texts.
note: Guidance is outside the uploaded texts; content left as is (reworded only). The underlying 211.110 text was verified under US-211-110.

requirement: Where appropriate, time limits for completing each production phase must be set to assure product quality. Exceeding a limit can be acceptable if quality is not compromised, but the departure must be justified and documented.
system_implications: The MBR defines named timers between start and end events. Tablets: wet-mass hold, granulation-to-drying, blend hold, coating-suspension hold, bulk hold before packaging. Injectables: start of compounding to sterilizing filtration, total filtration duration, sterilized equipment/component expiry before use, product exposure on the line, total aseptic filling duration, time between stoppering and capping, lyophilizer loading time, bulk hold. Timers run server-side (they survive client or network loss), warn before expiry, and on breach auto-create a deviation that needs justification and QA assessment. A breached timer is visible in review-by-exception and blocks release until dispositioned. Scope note: the specific timers listed (e.g., stoppering-to-capping, product exposure, sterilized-item expiry) are examples drawn from aseptic guidance and validation practice; the rule only requires time limits where appropriate plus justification and documentation of departures. Blocking release until the departure is dispositioned is consistent with 211.192.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: (a) For drug products that need not be sterile, appropriate written procedures designed to prevent objectionable microorganisms must be established and followed. (b) For products that purport to be sterile, appropriate written procedures designed to prevent microbiological contamination must be established and followed, and they must include validation of every aseptic and sterilization process.
system_implications: Tablets: enforce hold times and microbial controls defined in the MBR (e.g., aqueous granulation hold limits, purified water use-point sampling reference) and link water-system/utility status. Injectables: before sterilized items can be consumed, the system checks that each sterilization/depyrogenation/SIP cycle used a validated recipe ID and version for that load pattern and passed its acceptance criteria. Before aseptic operations start, the system checks that the filling line has a current successful aseptic process simulation, that assigned operators are APS-qualified, and that filters, sterilized equipment and components are within their validated hold times. Any failure is a hard stop. Scope notes: 211.113(b) requires the aseptic and sterilization processes to be validated; the specific gates (a current successful APS for the line, operator APS participation, filter and sterilized-item hold times) implement that requirement as described in FDA's 2004 aseptic processing guidance and are not spelled out in the rule. Purified-water sampling references and utility status for tablets are good practice under 211.113(a).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications labelled as guidance-derived where applicable.

requirement: Written, followed procedures must set out a system for reprocessing batches that fail standards or specifications, including the steps that make sure the reprocessed batch will meet all established standards, specifications and characteristics. Reprocessing may take place only after QCU review and approval.
system_implications: Reprocessing (and rework, if the company distinguishes them) can only be started from a QA-approved reprocessing instruction (MBR variant or protocol) linked to the non-conforming batch and its investigation. It creates a child execution record and genealogy edges (original lot -> reprocess -> resulting lot), so the resulting lot's history includes the original batch record. Production cannot initiate it alone. Reprocessed batches are flagged for enhanced testing and review and appear in APR data. Scope note: enhanced testing of reprocessed batches is good practice; the rule (with 211.165(f)) requires that reprocessed material meet appropriate standards and specifications before acceptance and use. 'Rework' is not a Part 211 term.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Written, followed procedures must describe in enough detail how labeling and packaging materials are received, identified, stored, handled, sampled, and examined and/or tested; these materials are sampled representatively and examined or tested on receipt and before use. Materials that meet their written specifications may be approved and released; those that do not are rejected so they cannot be used. For each shipment of each different labeling and packaging material, records show receipt, examination or testing, and acceptance or rejection. Labels and labeling for each different product, strength, dosage form or fill quantity are kept apart with suitable identification, in a store open only to authorized staff. Obsolete or outdated labels, labeling and other packaging materials are destroyed. Gang-printed labeling for different products, strengths or net contents is banned unless the sheets are clearly distinguished by size, shape or color. When cut labels are used on immediate containers, on individual unit cartons, or on multi-unit cartons whose immediate containers are not individually cartoned, one special control is required: (1) lines dedicated to each strength of each product; (2) electronic or electromechanical equipment that checks 100% of output for correct labeling during or after finishing; (3) for hand-applied labeling, a 100% visual check by one person, independently verified by a second; or (4) any automated method (label size or shape differentiation included) that physically stops wrong labeling from passing through the labeling and packaging equipment. Printing devices on or linked to the lines that imprint the unit label or case must be monitored so that every imprint matches what the BPR specifies.
system_implications: The packaging-material master links each item to an artwork version with QA approval. Only Released items of the current effective artwork version can be issued, and superseded versions are status-blocked and routed to destruction. Electronic 100% verification (vision/code readers): record device ID, recipe, and challenge-test results (known-good and known-bad samples) at start, at defined intervals and at end, plus counts inspected and rejected; a failed challenge blocks line start or continuation. Hand-applied labeling under (g)(3) records performer and an independent verifier. Variable-data printing (lot, expiry, NDC/GTIN, serial number, price if any) is compared electronically with the BPR data at start, at intervals and at end, and any mismatch stops the line. The first approved printed sample is captured as a specimen (211.188(b)(8)). Corrections (falls short): (1) the packaging master/MBR must record which 211.122(g) special control applies to each cut-labeling operation, and the system must support all four options, including dedicated lines ((g)(1)) and physical prevention by an automated technique such as size/shape differentiation ((g)(4)), not only vision systems and hand-applied checks. (2) Per-shipment receipt records for each labeling/packaging material (receipt, examination or testing, accept/reject) must exist in the eBMR or the integrated WMS/QMS (211.122(c), 211.184(d)). (3) Separate storage and restricted access for labels (211.122(d)) should be enforced through location/status and role checks at issuance. Scope notes: challenge-test timing (start/interval/end) is good practice, not stated in the rule; NDC/GTIN/serial print checks are driven by labeling rules and DSCSA outside the uploaded texts.
note: Corrected: the paraphrase listed only three of the four special-control options in 211.122(g) (omitting (g)(4), physical prevention by an automated technique), omitted the per-shipment receipt records required by (c), omitted which label/carton types (g) covers, and narrowed (e) to labels only (it also covers other packaging materials). Implications extended accordingly.

requirement: Labeling issued for labeling operations is strictly controlled. Labeling issued to a batch is carefully checked for identity and for conformity with the labeling specified in the master or batch records. Procedures balance the labeling quantities issued, used and returned, and call for evaluation whenever the difference between finished product quantity and labeling issued falls outside tight preset limits derived from historical operating data; such discrepancies are investigated under 211.192. Reconciliation is waived for cut or roll labeling when a 100% electronic or electromechanical examination under 211.122(g)(2) is performed. All surplus labeling printed with lot or control numbers is destroyed. Returned labeling is kept and stored so that mixups are prevented and it stays properly identified. Written procedures describing labeling issuance controls in sufficient detail are established and followed. (Documenting the issuance examination in the BPR is required by 211.130(d), 211.184(d) and 211.188(b)(8).)
system_implications: The issuance transaction records the counted quantity (or roll count/meters converted to units), the issuer and a verifier, and an examination step against the MBR specimen. The reconciliation form is computed by the system: Issued = Applied to finished units + Rejected/damaged + QC/retention samples + Returned to store + Destroyed. Product-to-label reconciliation is also computed. Reconciliation limits are configured per product/pack in the MBR with a recorded rationale (historical data reference) and change only under change control. Results outside the limits auto-create an investigation and block release. Destruction of lot-coded labeling is recorded with a witness. Returned uncoded labeling gets location and status tracking. The waiver applies only when the MBR declares 211.122(g)(2) electronic 100% examination and challenge records exist for the run. Scope notes: an issuer-plus-verifier count and a witness for destruction are good practice; the rule requires strict control, examination, reconciliation with investigation of out-of-limit discrepancies, destruction of lot-coded excess, and controlled storage of returns. The reconciliation waiver covers only cut or roll labeling examined under 211.122(g)(2); it does not extend to (g)(1), (g)(3) or (g)(4) controls.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; the original attributed documentation of the examination to 211.125(b), whereas that duty sits in 211.130(d), 211.184(d) and 211.188(b)(8). Implications correct; waiver scope clarified.

requirement: Written, followed procedures must make sure the correct labels, labeling and packaging materials are used, and must include: physical or spatial separation from operations on other products to prevent mixups and cross-contamination; identification and handling of filled containers held unlabeled for later labeling so that containers, lots or parts of lots are not mislabeled (identification need not be on each container but must allow name, strength, quantity and lot/control number to be determined); a lot or control number on the product that allows the batch's manufacturing and control history to be traced; checking before packaging starts that packaging and labeling materials are suitable and correct, recorded in the BPR; and inspecting the packaging and labeling facilities right before use to confirm that product from earlier operations and unsuitable materials have been removed, with results recorded in the BPR.
system_implications: A line-clearance checklist (configurable per line and room) is executed and e-signed before start (performer plus verifier per SOP) and after completion (211.188(b)(6)), and packaging cannot start without a completed pre-use clearance. A line may only have one active packaging order, lot and strength (spatial separation rule). Material verification at line start scans every packaging component against the packaging MBR bill of materials and artwork version. Unlabeled filled containers (e.g., unlabeled vials awaiting labeling, bulk tablets in drums) are tracked as quarantined intermediates with lot identity, quantity and container labels, and reconciled when later labeled. The lot number printed on each unit is the BPR lot number (no manual entry). Scope note: one active order per line is an implementation of the separation requirement; since the rule allows physical or spatial separation, adjacent lines separated by validated barriers can be configured.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

clause: 211.132(a)-(c) (with (d)-(f) for exemptions, NDA notification and PPPA)
requirement: Manufacturers and packers of OTC human drug products for retail sale (except dermatological, dentifrice, insulin and lozenge products) must use a tamper-evident package if the public can reach the product while it is held for sale; otherwise the product is adulterated and/or misbranded. The package needs one or more indicators or barriers to entry that, if breached or missing, would give consumers visible evidence of tampering; it must be distinctive by design or use an identifying characteristic (e.g., a pattern, name, trademark, logo or picture), and the feature must stay intact under reasonable handling through manufacture, distribution and retail display. Two-piece hard gelatin capsules must also be sealed with an acceptable tamper-evident technology. Each retail package (except ammonia inhalant in crushable glass ampules and gas-propelled aerosols) must carry a prominently placed statement, unaffected if the feature is breached or missing, that names all tamper-evident features and any capsule-sealing technology and refers to any identifying characteristic used. Exemptions require a citizen petition; NDA holders report related packaging and labeling changes under 314.70, and special packaging under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act still applies.
system_implications: For products flagged OTC, the packaging MBR must include tamper-evident feature controls, such as induction-seal integrity checks, torque checks and shrink-band presence (vision), and verification of the required tamper-evidence labeling statement. The MBR cannot be approved without these steps for OTC products. Corrections (falls short): the trigger is OTC retail status, not dosage form, so the product master needs an OTC-retail flag that drives these checks for any dosage form (tablets in this scope; insulin is exempt and most sterile injectables are prescription-only). Artwork approval must confirm that the tamper-evidence statement names every feature (and any capsule-sealing technology), refers to the identifying characteristic where one is used, is prominently placed and would survive a breach of the feature. If two-piece hard capsules are ever packaged, capsule-sealing verification is required.
note: Corrected (understated scope): the paraphrase omitted the distinctive-design/identifying-characteristic requirement, the capsule-sealing requirement, the content and placement rules for the labeling statement, and the exceptions to the statement. applies_to 'tablets' is a simplification; the rule is triggered by OTC retail status regardless of dosage form.

requirement: During finishing operations, packaged and labeled product is examined to give assurance that the containers and packages in the lot bear the correct label. When finishing is complete, a representative sample of units is collected and visually checked for correct labeling. The results of both examinations are recorded in the batch production or control records.
system_implications: Scheduled in-process label checks and a mandatory end-of-run representative sample examination step, with sample size per SOP (e.g., an AQL plan), examiner identity and result. A failure puts the lot on hold and opens an investigation. Results are included in the BPR (211.188(b)(13)). Scope note: AQL-based sampling is one acceptable way to define the representative sample; placing the lot on hold and opening an investigation on failure implements 211.192.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Each drug product must carry an expiration date, set by the stability testing of 211.166, so that it still meets its identity, strength, quality and purity standards at the time of use; the date must relate to any storage conditions stated on the labeling. Products reconstituted at dispensing need expiration information on the labeling for both the reconstituted and the unreconstituted product. Expiration dates appear on labeling as 21 CFR 201.17 requires (outside the uploaded texts). Exempt: homeopathic products; allergenic extracts labeled 'No U.S. Standard of Potency'; investigational new drugs that meet standards shown by stability studies during clinical use (reconstituted investigational products still need reconstituted-product expiry information). FDA does not enforce the section, pending a proposed exemption, for human OTC products whose labeling has no dosage limitations and that are shown stable for at least 3 years.
system_implications: The expiry rule (shelf-life months, reference event such as the date of first API addition or date of filling per company SOP, rounding such as last day of month) is product master data under change control. The expiry date is calculated once by the system and pushed identically to label print data, the BPR, ERP/WMS and serialization/DSCSA product identifier data; manual entry is prohibited. For lyophilized or powder-for-reconstitution injectables, artwork verification includes both unreconstituted and reconstituted (in-use) expiry statements. The BPR shows the storage-condition statement used. Scope notes: the rule does not fix the reference event for the dating period (e.g., first API addition or fill date); that comes from company policy and application commitments. Propagation to serialization/DSCSA data and the ban on manual entry are design choices beyond 211.137. If the eBMR is used for clinical supplies, configure the 211.137(g) exemption but still require reconstituted-product expiry where applicable.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; added (d) (labeling placement per 201.17) and spelled out the exemptions (e)-(h), which the original summarized loosely as 'certain OTC products'.

requirement: Every lot of components, drug product containers and closures is kept from use until the QCU has released it after appropriate sampling, testing or examination. Approved materials are retested or re-examined for identity, strength, quality and purity as needed (for instance after long storage or exposure to air, heat or other harmful conditions) and approved or rejected by the QCU under 211.84. Rejected materials are identified and controlled in a quarantine system designed to stop their use in operations for which they are unsuitable.
system_implications: Status-driven hard stops at every consumption point (dispensing, line-side issue, packaging component scan). Retest and expiry dates are enforced automatically: at the retest date the status reverts to Quarantine/Retest Required and the lot cannot be used until QA re-approves it. Rejected lots cannot be allocated or dispensed. Status changes are QA-only with e-signature. Partial containers inherit the lot status. Correction (falls short): 211.87 is event-driven as well as time-driven, so QA must also be able to send a released lot back to retest status after an adverse exposure (e.g., a warehouse temperature or humidity excursion, or damaged packaging), with the same hard stops applying. Scope note: fixed retest dates are good practice, not stated in the rule.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications fell short on event-triggered retesting under 211.87.

requirement: Drug product containers and closures must be clean and, where the drug's nature requires, sterilized and treated to remove pyrogenic properties so they are fit for use; depyrogenation processes must be validated. Written, followed standards or specifications and test methods, and where indicated cleaning, sterilizing and depyrogenation methods, are required for containers and closures. These container/closure provisions apply to all dosage forms (sterilization and depyrogenation only where the product requires them). For liquid filtration when making injectable drugs for human use, filters must not shed fibers; a fiber-releasing filter may be used only when the product cannot be made without it, and must then be followed by a non-fiber-releasing filter rated at most 0.2 micron nominal pore size (0.45 micron if manufacturing conditions require). Filters containing asbestos are prohibited.
system_implications: The BPR captures component preparation: washer run, depyrogenation tunnel run or oven cycle ID with validated recipe and result, sterilization cycle IDs for stoppers and equipment, and expiry of sterilized/depyrogenated items (hold time) at the point of use. Filters are verified by scan against the MBR-specified part number and pore size, and the filter lot is recorded. Pre-use (if performed) and post-use integrity test results are captured from the integrity tester with the raw report. A failed post-use integrity test is a critical event that blocks release pending investigation. Corrections: (1) 211.94(c) cleanliness and 211.94(d) specifications/test methods apply to all containers and closures, including tablet bottles, caps and blister films, so this line applies to both product types. (2) The filter master should carry 'non-fiber-releasing' and 'asbestos-free' attributes; if an MBR ever specifies a fiber-releasing filter, approval must require a downstream non-fiber-releasing filter of 0.2 micron (or 0.45 micron with justification). Scope note: filter integrity testing before/after use and the release block on a failed post-use test come from FDA's 2004 aseptic guidance and sterilizing-filtration validation (211.113(b)), not from 211.72.
note: Corrected: scope was set to injectables only, but 211.94(c)-(d) also cover tablet packaging components; the asbestos prohibition in 211.72 was omitted. Integrity-testing implications labelled as guidance-derived.

requirement: Written, followed distribution procedures must provide for shipping the oldest approved stock of a drug product first (temporary, appropriate departures allowed) and a system that makes each lot's distribution readily determinable so it can be recalled if necessary. Distribution records must show the product name and strength, a description of the dosage form, the consignee's name and address, the date and quantity shipped, and the lot or control number. (211.196 as currently worded after the June 2024 amendment.)
system_implications: The released-lot status flows from the eBMR to WMS/ERP. Shipment records are ingested as genealogy edges (lot -> shipment -> consignee) so a forward trace from any component, equipment or batch ends at consignees for recall scoping. FEFO deviations are recorded with reason. Correction: the rule's default is oldest approved stock first; if the SOP uses first-expiry-first-out instead, document why it achieves the same intent, and record reasons for any departure from the configured rule. Scope note: distribution normally runs in ERP/WMS; the eBMR's obligations are to publish released status and lot identity and to make the lot-to-consignee trace available for recalls and 211.192 investigations.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications used FEFO where the rule says oldest approved stock first; clarified.

requirement: Specifications, standards, sampling plans, test procedures and other laboratory control mechanisms, and changes to them, are drafted by the appropriate unit and reviewed and approved by the QCU; laboratory controls are followed and documented when performed, and departures are recorded and justified. Before release, each batch needs an appropriate laboratory determination that it meets final specifications, including identity and strength of each active ingredient (short-lived radiopharmaceuticals may be released before sterility/pyrogen tests finish, provided those tests are completed as soon as possible). Batches that must be free of objectionable microorganisms get appropriate microbial testing. Sampling and testing plans are written, state the sampling method and number of units tested per batch, and are followed. QCU acceptance criteria must be adequate to assure each batch meets every specification and appropriate statistical quality control criteria, including acceptance and/or rejection levels, as a condition of approval and release. Test methods have their accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility established and documented. Products failing standards, specifications or other quality criteria are rejected; reprocessed material must meet appropriate standards before acceptance and use. Every batch purporting to be sterile and/or pyrogen-free is tested for those attributes under written, followed procedures.
system_implications: The release gate (batch disposition) only allows the QA release e-signature when all mandatory criteria are met: BPR complete and QA-reviewed; all deviations and investigations closed or QA-assessed as not impacting; all required QC results complete and within specification (from LIMS, with specification version matching the MBR); label reconciliation and yields within limits (DSCSA serialization reconciliation is a DSCSA-driven addition, not Part 211). For aseptic products, sterility, endotoxin, container-closure/visual inspection results and EM/personnel monitoring review must also be complete. A terminally sterilized product with FDA-approved parametric release follows a separate criteria set defined by the application (US-TS-01 is not part of this set; parametric release is not addressed in the uploaded Part 211 text). Any exception to the gate exists only as a configured, SOP-backed 'conditional release for further processing/shipping under quarantine' with a recorded justification; it must never permit distribution before the 211.165(a) testing and the 211.192 review are complete. A rejected batch can never be released without a new approved reprocess path. Added: for controlled-release tablets the gate must include release-rate results for each active ingredient (211.167(c), see US-NEW-17), and the gate should confirm identity and strength results exist for every active ingredient (211.165(a)). Scope note: EM/personnel-monitoring review and visual-inspection results for aseptic products are guidance-derived gate items.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; added the QCU approval of laboratory control mechanisms in 211.160(a), the statistical acceptance/rejection levels in 211.165(d) and the reprocessed-material condition in 211.165(f). Implications: DSCSA and parametric release labelled as outside Part 211; conditional release limited; 211.167(c) gate item added.

requirement: (a) Production, control and distribution records required by Part 211 and specifically tied to a batch are kept for at least 1 year after that batch's expiration date or, for certain OTC products exempt from expiry dating under 211.137, 3 years after the batch is distributed. (b) Records for all components, containers, closures and labeling are kept at least 1 year after the expiration date (commonly read as the expiry of the last product lot that used them) or, for exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution of the last lot that used them. (c) All Part 211 records, or copies, must be readily available for authorized inspection during retention at the establishment where the activities took place and must be reproducible (e.g., photocopied) during inspection; records that the site can pull up instantly from elsewhere by computer or other electronic means count as available. (d) Records may be kept as originals or as true copies (e.g., photocopies, microfilm, microfiche or other accurate reproductions); if reduction techniques are used, suitable reader and copying equipment must be on hand.
system_implications: A retention engine computes the retention end date per record from genealogy. For a batch record: expiry + 1 year (or distribution + 3 years for exempt OTC). For shared records (component lot records, equipment logs, MBR versions, training, audit trails): the latest retention end of all dependent batches. Purge before that date is impossible, and legal holds override purge. Central multi-site hosting is acceptable if every site can retrieve its records immediately (defined retrieval SLA). Export produces true copies: PDF/A with signature manifestations and audit trail, plus native structured data and metadata. A migration strategy preserves content, meaning, metadata and audit trails across technology refreshes over retention periods that may exceed 10 years. Scope notes: 211.180 sets minimum periods tied to expiry or distribution; retention of training records and a 10+ year horizon come from other requirements or company policy. Audit-trail retention equal to the subject record comes from 11.10(e). Legal holds are good practice.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; added the (d) point on reader equipment for reduced copies. Implications consistent; retention drivers outside 211.180 labelled.

requirement: Written records must be kept so their data can support an evaluation, at least once a year, of the quality standards of each drug product, to decide whether its specifications or its manufacturing or control procedures need to change. Written, followed procedures for this review must cover a representative number of batches (approved or rejected) and, where applicable, their associated records, plus complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged products, and 211.192 investigations for each product.
system_implications: All CPPs, IPCs, yields, deviations, reprocessing and release decisions are stored as structured, typed data with units and specification version, not free text, and are queryable across batches, sites and time for APR/PQR and CPV (US-PV-01). The system provides APR data extracts with provenance (source record IDs and hashes), and links to complaints, recalls and returns by lot. Scope note: CPV and data-provenance hashes are guidance-derived or design choices (US-PV-01 is not in this set); the rule requires that records be usable for the annual review. Added: returned and salvaged product records (211.204, 211.208) and recalls must be linkable by lot so the review can include them (see US-NEW-21 and US-NEW-22).
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; linkage to returned/salvaged product records added.

requirement: Cleaning, maintenance (other than routine lubrication and adjustments) and use of major equipment are recorded in individual equipment logs that record, for every batch processed, its lot number and product plus the date and time. Individual logs are not needed for equipment dedicated to one product if its lots follow, and are made in, numerical sequence, but then the cleaning, maintenance and use records belong in the batch record. The person doing the cleaning or maintenance and the person double-checking it date and sign or initial the log (for cleaning or maintenance done by automated equipment under 211.68, only the verifying person). Log entries are kept in chronological order.
system_implications: The electronic equipment logbook is populated automatically from eBMR events (use start/stop with product and lot), cleaning records (performer plus a different verifier, or one verifier for a validated automated CIP/SIP cycle) and maintenance work orders (via CMMS interface). Entries are ordered by actual event time. Late or out-of-sequence entries require a reason and are flagged, and the original chronology is preserved. Entries are immutable with an audit-trailed correction mechanism. For dedicated equipment, the logbook extract is embedded in the batch report and the system checks the numerical lot sequence.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Component, container, closure and labeling records must include: (a) for each shipment of each lot, its identity and quantity, the supplier name, the supplier lot number(s) if known, the 211.80 receiving code, the receipt date and, if known and different from the supplier, the name and location of the prime manufacturer; (b) the results of every test or examination (including those under 211.82(a), 211.84(d) and 211.122(a)) and the conclusions drawn; (c) an individual inventory record for each component, container and closure and, for components, a reconciliation of the use of each lot, with enough information to identify every drug product batch or lot that used each component, container or closure; (d) documentation that labels and labeling were examined and reviewed for conformity with specifications (see 211.122(c) and 211.130(c)); (e) a record of what was done with rejected components, containers, closures and labeling.
system_implications: An append-only inventory ledger per container/lot records receipt, sampling, status changes, dispensing, returns, waste and adjustments (with reason and verifier). A lot reconciliation report is computed: received = consumed + sampled + returned to vendor + destroyed + on hand, with adjustments explained. Genealogy edges from every consumption transaction support forward traceability (component lot -> all drug product lots), which 211.184(c) makes mandatory. Correction (falls short): the receipt record must also hold the supplier lot number(s), the receiving code and the prime manufacturer's name and location when it differs from the supplier (211.184(a)); container and closure lots need individual inventory records and batch traceability too (211.184(c)), even though the lot reconciliation is required only for components; and the disposition of rejected materials, including labeling, must be recorded (211.184(e)).
note: Corrected: the paraphrase omitted the prime-manufacturer name/location data element in 211.184(a). Implications extended with the missing data elements.

requirement: To keep batches uniform, a master production and control record is needed for each drug product and for each of its batch sizes; one person prepares, dates and signs it with a full handwritten signature, and a second person independently checks, dates and signs it. A written, followed procedure describes how these records are prepared. Under 11.1(c), an electronic signature that meets Part 11 counts as equivalent to a full handwritten signature (211.186(a) predates the August 1997 cut-off for exceptions), so a compliant e-signature satisfies this; the FDA data integrity Q&A says the same but is guidance.
system_implications: The MBR authoring workflow requires an Author e-signature ('Prepared'), an independent Checker e-signature ('Checked'; must differ from the author), and QA approval ('Approved', per 211.22(c)/211.100(a)), with an effective date. Versioning and supersession are handled with a redline comparison between versions. Only Effective versions can issue batch records, and in-flight batches stay on their issued version. The MBR is defined per approved batch size. Scaling is allowed only to batch sizes that each have an approved master record. A 'validated range' approach is acceptable only if the approved master record states the component quantities for every batch size actually produced (211.186(a) requires a master record for each batch size); never ad hoc. Changes go through change control with impact assessment. Scope note: the QA 'Approved' signature comes from 211.100(a) and 211.22(c); 211.186(a) itself requires the preparer's and the independent checker's signatures.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. The binding basis for accepting e-signatures here is 11.1(c) in the uploaded Part 11 text; the DI Q&A is supporting guidance. Implication on batch-size ranges tightened because 211.186(a) requires a master record for each batch size.

requirement: The master record must contain: the product name, strength and dosage-form description; each active ingredient's name and quantity, expressed per dosage unit or per weight/volume unit of product, and the total weight or measure of one dosage unit; a complete component list using names or codes specific enough to show any special quality characteristic; an accurate amount for each component, all expressed in one weight system (metric, avoirdupois or apothecary), with reasonable variations allowed only if justified in the record; a statement of any calculated excess of a component; theoretical weight or measure at appropriate processing phases; theoretical yield together with the upper and lower percentage limits that trigger a 211.192 investigation; a description of containers, closures and packaging materials, plus a sample or copy of every label and other labeling piece bearing the approver's signature and date; and full manufacturing and control instructions together with the sampling and test procedures, specifications, and any special notes and precautions.
system_implications: The MBR data model has mandatory structured fields for all nine elements. Validation rules block approval if any element is missing: one weight system (e.g., metric) used consistently across all components of the record, with unit prefixes (mg, g, kg) allowed within it; overage fields with justification text; yield limits mandatory at each yield checkpoint; label specimens linked to approved artwork with approver signatures; instructions as structured steps with parameters and limits, IPC/sampling plans and specification references; hazard/precaution notations. Component codes must reference material master records carrying quality grade (e.g., 'WFI', 'low-endotoxin', 'micronized'). Scope note: enforcing structured fields is a design choice; the rule requires the content, not its format.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct (the meta-comment about verbatim confirmation was dropped). Implication corrected: 211.186(b)(4) requires the same weight system across the components, not a single unit per component.

requirement: A batch production and control record must be prepared for every batch, holding complete information on its production and control, and must start from a faithful copy of the relevant master record, with that copy checked for accuracy, dated and signed. (Controlled issuance and reconciliation of blank forms comes from the FDA 2018 data integrity Q&A, i.e., guidance outside the uploaded texts; in an eBMR its equivalent is controlled issuance of batch record instances.)
system_implications: A batch record instance is generated only from the Effective MBR version; the MBR version ID and content hash are stored in the instance. An issuance e-signature ('Issued/verified accurate reproduction') is required. Once issued, instruction content is frozen: later MBR changes do not alter it, and any batch-specific change needs a controlled, QA-approved amendment. Batch record instances are uniquely numbered and reconciled (issued vs executed vs voided). Voided or reissued instances are kept with reason and approver, never deleted.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; the blank-form statement is guidance (outside the uploaded texts) and is labelled as such. Implications correct.

requirement: The batch record must document that each significant step of manufacture, processing, packing or holding was accomplished, covering: the dates; which individual major equipment and lines were used; specific identification of each component or in-process material batch used; component weights and measures used during processing; in-process and laboratory control results; checks of the packaging/labeling area both before and after it is used; actual yield and percentage of theoretical yield at appropriate phases; complete labeling control records with specimens or copies of all labeling used; a description of containers and closures; any sampling performed; who performed each significant step and who directly supervised or checked it (or, for a step done by automated equipment under 211.68, who checked the equipment's work); any 211.192 investigation; and the results of the 211.134 label examinations.
system_implications: Steps are flagged as 'significant' in the MBR, and each flagged step requires a performer signature plus a verifier/supervisor signature from a different user (or automated execution plus one checker). The batch report must render all 13 data categories. A completeness engine blocks 'Production complete' if any category is missing: sampling events with sample IDs linked to LIMS, label specimens (image of the first printed label or scan), container/closure descriptions from master data, and investigations linked. Dates and times come from server timestamps. Clarifications: the completeness engine must test only the categories applicable to the step type (e.g., packaging-area inspections only for packaging), and specimens must cover all labeling used (labels, cartons, inserts), not only the first printed label. Scope note: a second person on every significant step matches (b)(11) ('directly supervising or checking'); for automated steps one checker suffices per 211.68(c).
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; small clarifications on applicability and labeling specimens.

requirement: Before a batch is released or distributed, the QCU must review and approve all its production and control records, packaging and labeling records included, to establish compliance with all established, approved written procedures. Any unexplained discrepancy (including a percentage of theoretical yield outside the master-record limits), or any failure of a batch or its components to meet specifications, requires a thorough investigation, even if the batch has already shipped, and that investigation must extend to other batches of the same product and to other products that may be associated with the failure or discrepancy. A written investigation record with conclusions and follow-up is required.
system_implications: A QA review workbench does review-by-exception. It lists every deviation, out-of-limit value, late entry, correction of critical data (from the audit trail, per the DI Q&A), manual fallback/override, alarm, timer breach and open item. Each exception must be individually acknowledged or dispositioned before release. The full record stays viewable, because review-by-exception supplements full-record access and does not replace it. The investigation module (or QMS link) has a mandatory impact-assessment step. The system supplies impact queries: other batches sharing component lots, intermediate lots, equipment (and the previous/next product), rooms, personnel, utilities, time windows, APS or EM excursions, and other products made on the same equipment. Investigations require conclusion and follow-up/CAPA fields. Post-distribution investigations can be linked to distributed lots and their consignees. Scope notes: routine review of critical-data audit trails before release and per-exception acknowledgment come from FDA data-integrity guidance and design choices, not 211.192 text; CAPA fields are good practice (the rule requires conclusions and follow-up). Review-by-exception is acceptable only because the QCU still approves the complete record, so the release e-signature meaning should state that the full record was reviewed.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; guidance-derived elements labelled.

requirement: Laboratory records must contain complete data from every test needed to assure compliance with specifications and standards, including: a description of each sample with its source (where it was taken), quantity, lot number or other distinctive code, date sampled and date received for testing; a statement of each test method used, with the location of data showing the method is accurate and reliable for the product (a citation suffices for unmodified compendial, AOAC, other recognized or approved-application methods), plus verification that every method is suitable under actual conditions of use; the sample weight or measure used for each test where appropriate; a complete record of all raw data, including instrument graphs, charts and spectra, each identified to the specific material and lot tested; all calculations with units, conversion and equivalency factors; the results and how they compare with the standards; the tester's initials or signature and the test dates; and a second person's initials or signature confirming the original records were checked for accuracy, completeness and compliance.
system_implications: For IPCs executed in the eBMR (weights, hardness, pH, fill volume), the system stores raw instrument output (files or strings) linked to instrument ID, sample ID and the step, the calculation with formula version, the result vs limits, and performer and date. A second-person review of IPC data is required where the SOP classifies the test as a laboratory test. Result-only entry is not allowed when the instrument can transmit raw data. Invalidated or repeated measurements are retained with justification (US-DI-10). Corrections (falls short): IPC records must also capture the test method reference and version (with the location of its validation/suitability data), the sample quantity used where relevant, units and conversion factors in calculations, and a link from the raw data to the specific material and lot tested (not only to the instrument). Whether shop-floor IPCs count as laboratory records is a firm decision that must be justified; if they do, the second-person review in (a)(8) is mandatory, and in any case 211.188(b)(11) requires a checker for significant steps.
