Scope notes: 'no result-only entry' is a design choice; US-DI-10 is not part of this set.
note: Corrected: (a)(4) requires the data (graphs, charts, spectra) to be identified to the material and lot tested; the paraphrase shifted this to 'properly identified instrumentation'. Also restored the omitted date received for testing, the method-validation location/citation rule and the suitability-under-actual-use requirement of (a)(2), and units/factors in (a)(5).

requirement: Written, followed procedures must govern handling of all written and oral complaints about a drug product, including QCU review of any complaint about a possible failure to meet specifications, a decision on whether a 211.192 investigation is needed, and a review of whether the complaint is a serious and unexpected adverse drug experience that must be reported under 21 CFR 310.305 or 514.80. Each complaint is recorded in a designated complaint file kept at the establishment that made, processed or packed the product, or elsewhere if the records are readily available for inspection there. Where known, the record gives product name and strength, lot number, complainant name, nature of the complaint and the reply. If investigated, the record includes findings and follow-up (the investigation record itself stays where the investigation was done, per 211.180(c)); if not, it gives the reason and names the person who decided no investigation was needed. Complaint records are kept for the later of 1 year after the product's expiry or 1 year after receipt of the complaint; for OTC products exempt from expiry dating, 3 years after distribution.
system_implications: A complaint lot lookup must immediately retrieve the full BPR, genealogy, deviations and distribution for the lot, and the eBMR exposes an API for the QMS complaint module. Complaint-to-lot links feed APR (211.180(e)) and extend batch-record retention if the complaint's retention end is later. Correction (goes beyond): 211.198(b) sets the retention of the complaint record itself; it does not require extending batch-record retention, so auto-extension is a design choice (useful where the complaint file relies on the batch record). Scope note: the complaint workflow normally sits in the QMS; the eBMR's regulatory role is fast lot lookup and links for investigations and the annual review.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; retention wording now verified against the uploaded text. Added the omitted adverse-drug-experience reportability review in (a) and the file-location rules. Implication on extending batch-record retention flagged as beyond the rule.

requirement: Part 11 sets the criteria for FDA to regard electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures applied to electronic records as reliable, trustworthy and broadly equivalent to paper records with handwritten signatures. It covers any record kept in electronic form (created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted) under an FDA records requirement, but not paper records that have merely been sent electronically. Computer systems (hardware and software), controls and associated documentation kept under Part 11 must be open to FDA inspection and readily available to inspectors. For records kept but not submitted to FDA, electronic records and signatures may replace paper and handwritten signatures in whole or in part if Part 11 is met (11.2(a)). Definitions: in a closed system, access is controlled by the people responsible for the records' content; in an open system it is not. Other defined terms include electronic record, electronic signature (symbols an individual executes, adopts or authorizes as the legally binding equivalent of a handwritten signature), digital signature (cryptographic, allowing signer identity and data integrity to be verified), biometrics, and handwritten signature (which also covers a scripted name or legal mark applied with a stylus to a capturing device).
system_implications: Every 211 record held in the eBMR is a Part 11 record. Validation documentation, configuration specifications, SOPs and supplier documentation must be inspection-ready at each site (11.1(e)). Classify the deployment as a closed system: for vendor-hosted or multi-tenant SaaS, access control, identity provisioning and privileged access must stay under the regulated company's control (contractually and technically), with vendor/admin access logged and approved. If that cannot be demonstrated, apply 11.30: the applicable 11.10 controls plus additional measures such as document encryption and digital signature standards as needed for the circumstances (11.30 gives these as examples, not a fixed pair).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; filled in what the cited 11.2 and 11.3(b) definitions actually say (the original listed them without content) and the 11.1(b) carve-out for paper records sent electronically. Implication corrected: 11.30 requires the 11.10 controls plus extra measures as needed, with encryption and digital signatures given only as examples.

requirement: Closed systems must be validated to show that they are accurate and reliable, perform consistently as intended, and can detect records that are invalid or have been altered.
system_implications: Risk-based validation (see US-CSA-01) with traceability from the URS (this requirement set) to test evidence. Technical means to discern altered records: cryptographic content hashes on each record version and signature, a hash-chained append-only audit trail, and a scheduled integrity-verification job that recomputes chains and alarms on mismatch. Site-specific configuration baselines are compared against the validated baseline to detect configuration drift. Scope notes: cryptographic hashing, hash chains and integrity jobs are design choices that serve the ability to detect altered records; the rule does not prescribe them. Risk-based/CSA validation (US-CSA-01, not in this set) is FDA guidance.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: The system must be able to output full, accurate copies of its records, both as human-readable renderings and in electronic form, suitable for FDA to inspect, review and copy; firms should contact FDA with any questions about the agency's ability to review and copy the records.
system_implications: One-click export of the complete batch record: human-readable (PDF/A including all data, signature manifestations, deviations, attachments and the audit trail) and electronic (structured JSON/XML/CSV with metadata, plus native attachments). Exports are themselves logged (who, when, what). For dynamic data (process trends, chromatograms, lyophilizer cycle data), provide the data plus a viewer and the static rendering. Supports FDA records requests under FD&C Act 704(a)(4) and remote regulatory assessments. Scope note: logging of exports and support for FD&C Act 704(a)(4) requests and remote assessments are good practice or other-statute drivers outside the uploaded texts.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Records must be protected so they can be retrieved accurately and readily for the whole retention period.
system_implications: Immutable storage for finalized records (object lock/WORM), geo-redundant backups, periodic restore tests, and format-longevity policy (open formats such as PDF/A and JSON with schema versions). Periodic readability tests of the oldest archived records. Documented and validated data migrations with before/after hash reconciliation. Retention is tied to US-211-180.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; the named storage technologies are design choices.

requirement: Access to the system must be limited to authorized individuals.
system_implications: Unique named accounts only, with no generic or shared accounts (see US-DI-04). Identity provider/SSO integration with MFA is acceptable. Joiner/mover/leaver provisioning tied to HR, with immediate disablement on termination. Periodic access recertification by area owners. Session inactivity timeout and auto-lock on shop-floor terminals. Break-glass accounts are sealed, alarmed and reviewed. Scope note: HR-driven provisioning, access recertification and inactivity locks are good-practice ways of meeting this; inactivity locks also matter for defining a continuous period of controlled access under 11.200(a)(1). US-DI-04 is not part of this set.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: The system must use secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that capture on their own the date and time of each operator entry or action that creates, changes or deletes an electronic record. A change must leave the previously recorded information visible. Audit trail documentation is kept at least as long as the underlying electronic records and is available to FDA for review and copying.
system_implications: The audit trail is generated server-side, independent of the application UI, and is append-only. Each entry captures: who (unique user ID plus printed name at the time), what (record, field, old value, new value), when (UTC server timestamp plus site time zone), why (reason for change, mandatory for any modification of GMP data after initial commit, chosen from a controlled list plus free text), and where (terminal/device ID). Nobody, including administrators, can edit, delete or disable audit trails on GMP objects; audit configuration changes are themselves audited and alarmed. Corrections create new record versions and the original value stays visible. GMP records are never physically deleted in normal operation; they are voided or invalidated with a reason. Audit trail retention equals record retention. The audit trail is searchable, filterable by batch, step, user and critical data, and exportable. Hash chaining provides tamper evidence. Record-level and system-level events (logins, failed logins, permission changes, configuration changes) are captured too, per the DI Q&A definition. Scope notes (beyond 11.10(e)): a mandatory reason for change comes from FDA guidance and EU Annex 11, not from 11.10(e); device ID capture is good practice (related to 11.10(h)); login and failed-login logging supports 11.300(d) rather than 11.10(e). A ban on physical deletion is a design choice (11.10(e) assumes deletions can occur but must be audit-trailed without obscuring prior data). Hash chaining is a design choice.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; flagged implication items that come from guidance or other clauses.

requirement: Where appropriate, operational system checks must enforce the permitted order of steps and events.
system_implications: An MBR execution state machine enforces step order (with MBR-declared parallel branches) and prerequisites: line clearance, equipment status, material status, IPC due, timer states, QA gates. The batch lifecycle (Issued -> In Execution -> Production Complete -> Under QA Review -> Released/Rejected, with Hold and Cancelled) has guarded transitions. Out-of-sequence execution is only possible via a deviation path with QA approval, and is recorded. Scope note: the QA-approved deviation path for out-of-sequence execution is a design choice; the rule only requires sequencing checks where appropriate.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Authority checks must confirm that a person is authorized before letting them use the system, sign a record electronically, reach the operation or the system's input/output devices, change a record, or carry out the operation in question.
system_implications: Fine-grained, least-privilege permissions per action (execute, verify, supervise, QA review, approve MBR, change master data, configure, administer), scoped by legal entity, site, area, product and line. Signature meanings are bound to roles (a user without QA role cannot sign 'Approved for release'). Segregation-of-duties rules: performer is not verifier; author is not checker; executor is not QA approver for the same batch; administrator is not a GMP data user on the same system unless an approved exception with a second reviewer applies (per the DI Q&A). Cross-site data isolation is enforced by default. Scope note: the segregation-of-duties rules 'executor is not QA approver' and 'administrator is not a GMP data user' are good practice from FDA data-integrity guidance; 11.10(g) itself requires authority checks, while 'performer is not verifier' and 'author is not checker' come from the Part 211 second-person rules (211.101, 211.103, 211.186(a), 211.188(b)(11)).
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; sources of the segregation-of-duties rules clarified.

requirement: Where appropriate, device (e.g., terminal) checks must confirm that the source of data input or operational instructions is valid.
system_implications: Registered devices only: terminals, tablets, scales, instruments and PLC/SCADA connectors carry device identities (certificates or IDs) and are assigned to a room or line. Data is accepted only from a device registered to the location of the executing step. Each value stores its source device ID. Operational instructions sent to equipment (recipe download) go only to the registered equipment for that step. Scope note: binding every device to a location is one way to meet the 'as appropriate' device checks; the rule does not require it for all devices.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: (i) It must be established that the people who develop, maintain or use the electronic record/signature system have the education, training and experience for their assigned tasks. (j) Written policies, established and followed, must make individuals accountable and responsible for actions taken under their electronic signatures, so that record and signature falsification is deterred. (k) Systems documentation must be appropriately controlled: its distribution, access and use for system operation and maintenance must be controlled, and revision and change control procedures must keep an audit trail showing, in time order, how that documentation was developed and modified.
system_implications: (i) Training records cover end users, key users, administrators and vendor developers (supplier qualification). (j) Before first signing, each user electronically acknowledges the e-signature accountability statement, and the acknowledgment is recorded and a prerequisite for signing; it is refreshed periodically. (k) System documentation (URS, configuration specifications, SOPs, admin manuals) lives in a controlled document system. Configuration changes are versioned with diffs and linked to change records, and the system's own configuration audit trail is retained. Scope note: an electronic acknowledgment before first signing and its periodic refresh are good-practice ways to show adherence to the 11.10(j) policy; the text does not require them.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Anyone using an open system to create, modify, maintain or transmit electronic records must apply procedures and controls that protect the records' authenticity, integrity and, where appropriate, confidentiality from creation until receipt. These include the 11.10 controls as appropriate plus additional measures, such as document encryption and suitable digital signature standards, as needed in the circumstances.
system_implications: Apply to any record flow crossing organizational boundaries or the public internet outside the company's access control: CMO/CDMO data exchange, DSCSA EPCIS exchange with trading partners, remote vendor support, FDA submissions. Use TLS 1.2+ in transit, encryption at rest, message-level signing (e.g., signed payloads or digital signatures) for data exchanged with third parties, and certificate management. Clarification: whether a system is open or closed depends on who controls access, not on the network used; 11.30 also requires the applicable 11.10 controls, not only encryption and signing. DSCSA EPCIS exchange is a DSCSA driver outside the uploaded texts.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Signed electronic records must show, with each signing, the signer's printed name, the date and time of signing, and what the signature means (e.g., review, approval, responsibility or authorship). These three items are controlled in the same way as the electronic records themselves and must appear in every human-readable form of the record, such as a screen display or printout.
system_implications: Every signature is displayed and printed with: full printed name (not just the user ID), date and time including time zone (store UTC; show site-local with offset), and a meaning from a controlled list bound to the step ('Performed by', 'Verified by', 'Supervised/Checked by', 'Reviewed by QA', 'Approved for release', 'Rejected', 'Prepared', 'Checked', 'Approved'). The manifestation is stored immutably with the signature at signing time, not re-derived from the mutable user table, so later name changes do not alter historic signatures. Manifestations appear on every screen and report view of the signed data.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures applied to electronic records, must be linked to their records so that nobody can, by ordinary means, remove, copy or transfer a signature to falsify an electronic record.
system_implications: Each signature record binds the signer identity, meaning, timestamp and a cryptographic hash of the exact signed content (the record version). A later permitted correction of signed data automatically marks the signature 'superseded by change' and requires re-signing (the performer's or verifier's as applicable), with the audit trail kept. Signatures cannot be moved or copied between records, and the integrity job detects any such tampering. Hybrid wet-ink signatures on printouts are avoided. If unavoidable, the scanned signed page is indexed to the record ID and content hash and the hybrid process is covered by an SOP. Scope note: cryptographic content hashes and automatic re-signing after a correction exceed the 'ordinary means' standard of 11.70; they are sound design choices, not requirements.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: (a) Each electronic signature belongs to exactly one individual and is never reused by or reassigned to anyone else. (b) The organization verifies a person's identity before it establishes, assigns, certifies or otherwise sanctions that person's electronic signature or any element of it. (c) Before or when they first use them, persons using electronic signatures certify to FDA that the signatures in their system (used on or after 20 August 1997) are meant to be legally binding like traditional handwritten signatures; the certification carries a traditional handwritten signature and is sent electronically or on paper, with submission details on FDA's Letters of Non-Repudiation Agreement web page. On request, they give FDA additional certification or testimony that a particular e-signature legally binds the signer as a handwritten one would.
system_implications: User IDs are never reused or reassigned, even after deactivation; enforced by a permanent uniqueness registry across all sites and tenants. Account activation requires a recorded identity-verification step (who verified, method, date). A go-live checklist per legal entity records the non-repudiation letter submission (date, scope: company-wide or individual). Signature credentials are personal: no proxy signing or delegated signing on behalf of another person. Scope note: 11.100(c) is an organizational submission, not a system function; tracking it in a go-live checklist is good practice.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct, including the 2023 amendment to (c)(1) as shown in the uploaded text.

requirement: Electronic signatures not based on biometrics must use at least two distinct identification components (such as an ID code and a password). Within one continuous period of controlled system access, the first signing uses all components and later signings use at least one component that only the individual can execute and that is meant for that individual's use alone; signings made outside such a continuous period each use all components. Non-biometric signatures may be used only by their genuine owners and must be administered and executed so that any attempt by someone else to use them would need two or more people to collude. Biometric signatures must be designed so that nobody other than their genuine owner can use them.
system_implications: The signing dialog re-authenticates at the moment of signing (user ID + password, or an SSO step-up with a second factor). The 'continuous period of controlled access' is defined strictly: any lock, timeout, logout or terminal switch ends it. Recommendation: require both components for all critical signatures (verification, QA review, release, MBR approval), because shop-floor terminals are shared. A verifier signs in the same dialog with their own full credentials; the performer's session can never supply the verifier's signature. No 'remember password'. Administrators cannot see passwords, and admin-set passwords force a change at first use (so misuse needs collusion). Biometric options, such as badge plus fingerprint in cleanrooms where typing is impractical, need liveness and anti-spoofing evidence.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; the rule to require both components for all critical signatures is correctly labelled as a recommendation.

requirement: Where e-signatures rely on ID codes combined with passwords, controls must protect their security and integrity, including: keeping every ID-code/password combination unique to one person; periodically checking, recalling or revising issued codes and passwords (e.g., password aging); procedures for managing losses, so that tokens, cards or other devices that hold or generate codes/passwords and are lost, stolen, missing or possibly compromised are electronically deauthorized, with temporary or permanent replacements issued under rigorous controls; transaction safeguards that prevent unauthorized use of passwords or ID codes and that detect any attempted misuse and report it immediately and urgently to the system security unit and, where appropriate, to management; and initial and periodic testing of such tokens or cards to confirm they work and have not been altered without authorization.
system_implications: Password policy: complexity, history, and aging or a documented risk-based equivalent (e.g., NIST SP 800-63B with compromised-password screening), with the rationale recorded. Account lockout after N failed login or signature attempts. Real-time security alerting (SIEM) on repeated failures, signature attempts on locked accounts, and anomalous access, routed to the security unit with acknowledgment tracking and escalation to management. Immediate revocation of lost badges or tokens, with replacement issued only after identity verification. Periodic badge and token functional tests. Clarification: if password aging is replaced by a NIST-style risk-based policy, 11.300(b) still requires periodic checking of issued credentials (e.g., access recertification and compromised-credential screening); document how that is met.
note: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

clause: FDA Guide to Inspections of Lyophilization of Parenterals (1993) - not in the uploaded texts; the 211.137(c) citation was verified
requirement: FDA's 1993 investigator guide on lyophilization of parenterals covers the freeze-drying cycle and its controls, cycle validation, and lyophilizer sterilization and design; cycle records are reviewed against the validated/filed cycle (details from recollection, not verified here). The one Part 211 citation, 211.137(c), is confirmed: products reconstituted at dispensing need labeled expiry information for both the reconstituted and the unreconstituted forms.
system_implications: Integrate the lyophilizer SCADA/historian: recipe ID and version, and per-phase setpoints and actuals (shelf temperature, chamber pressure, condenser temperature, product thermocouple/wireless probe temperatures, pressure-rise or comparative pressure tests, phase durations). Record loading pattern and time, stoppering, and chamber sterilization/leak-test status before loading. Excursions against validated ranges auto-create deviations. Loading/unloading times feed time-limit timers. Store native cycle data as dynamic records (US-DI-08). Anchors in the uploaded Part 211 text for these controls: 211.113(b) (validated sterilization and aseptic processes, covering chamber sterilization), 211.68(a) (routine calibration/checks of the lyophilizer and its sensors), 211.111 (time limits such as loading and unloading), 211.188(b)(5) and (b)(11) (process results and the person checking automated steps). US-DI-08 is not part of this set.
note: Guide is outside the uploaded texts and left as is (reworded only); the 211.137(c) reference was verified and in-text anchors added.

requirement: Within Part 211, traceability is required as follows. Backward: the lot or control number must allow the batch's manufacturing and control history to be determined (211.130(c)), and the batch record must identify the major equipment, the component and in-process lots used, and the people who performed and checked each significant step (211.188(b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(11); 211.105(b)). Forward: component, container and closure inventory records must identify every product lot that used them (211.184(c)); equipment logs must show each batch processed (211.182); and the distribution of each lot must be readily determinable for recall (211.150(b), 211.196). Investigations must reach other batches and products possibly associated with a failure or discrepancy (211.192). The wording 'complete history including distribution' belongs to the Part 210 lot-number definition (outside the uploaded texts), and serial-number/aggregation traceability comes from DSCSA (outside). Room-level and person-level forward tracing are not explicit requirements; they are useful for 211.192 impact assessments.
system_implications: This answers the user's question on graph-based data structures and databases; the recommendation below is engineering judgment, not regulatory text. Genealogy is inherently a directed, time-stamped multigraph. Nodes: material lots, sublots/containers, batches/steps, equipment units, rooms, persons, sterilizer loads, EM samples, serial numbers, cases, pallets, shipments, consignees, deviations. Edges: consumed-by, produced, split/merge, used-equipment, performed-by, sterilized-in, aggregated-into, shipped-in, relates-to-investigation. Queries are variable-depth (multi-stage API -> granulate -> tablets -> coated -> packaged; rework; blending of several intermediate lots; inter-site transfers), so graph modelling fits naturally. The same regulations also set outcomes that constrain the design, though they do not prescribe technologies: unreleased material must not be used and second-person checks must be enforced (211.84(a), 211.101); audit trails must be secure, computer-generated and time-stamped and must not obscure prior entries (11.10(e)); signatures must be linked so they cannot be excised, copied or transferred by ordinary means (11.70); backups must be exact, complete and secure (211.68(b)); records must stay retrievable and copyable for their retention period, which 211.180 sets at a minimum of 1 year after batch expiry (3 years after distribution for exempt OTC), so any 10+ year horizon is a business or other-regulation assumption; and the system must be validated (11.10(a), 211.68(b)). ACID transactions, append-only ledgers and cryptographic binding are engineering choices that meet these outcomes. Recommended pattern: (1) The system of record is an ACID store (relational, e.g., PostgreSQL, or equivalent) with an append-only, hash-chained event/transaction ledger. Genealogy edges are written in the same transaction as the business event (e.g., a consumption record), so the graph can never disagree with the batch record and there is no dual-write inconsistency. (2) Most genealogy queries run fine as recursive queries (SQL recursive CTEs, or SQL/PGQ property-graph queries where the RDBMS supports them) on indexed edge tables. DSCSA aggregation is shallow (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) but high-volume (millions of serials per batch), which relational parent-pointer tables handle well. (3) If scale or latency across many sites needs a dedicated graph database for investigation or recall analytics, make it a derived, read-only, rebuildable projection (CQRS) fed from the ledger via outbox/CDC. Add automated reconciliation (edge counts and hashes per lot) and treat it as GMP-relevant, validated software if its outputs drive GMP decisions such as investigation scope or recall lists. Never make it the sole store of signed records unless it provides equivalent Part 11 audit trail, immutability, point-in-time recovery and long-term export, which most graph databases do not offer natively. (4) Keep genealogy bitemporal (valid time and recording time), so the graph 'as known at release' can be reconstructed after later corrections. (5) Use globally unique IDs with site-scoped business lot numbers to support multi-site graphs, and partition operational data by site with a global genealogy index. 211.180(c) permits central electronic retrieval. (6) The MBR/recipe structure (ISA-88 procedure -> unit procedure -> operation -> phase, with parallel branches) is a DAG that can live as versioned structured documents inside the relational store; it does not require a graph database.
note: Corrected: anchors made precise; the implications claimed the regulations 'require' ACID transactions, cryptographic signature binding and 10+ year retention, which overstates them (these are design choices, and 211.180 sets a shorter minimum). Room/person traceability flagged as good practice. The architecture recommendation itself is engineering judgment and was left intact.

requirement: Taken together: entries are documented when the work is performed (211.100(b), 211.160(a)) and identify who performed and who checked each significant step (211.188(b)(11)); secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails record operator entries and actions, keep earlier information visible and are retained as long as the records (11.10(e)); signed records show printed name, date/time and meaning (11.50); signatures are linked to their records so they cannot be excised, copied or transferred by ordinary means (11.70); backups are exact, complete and protected from alteration, erasure or loss (211.68(b)); the system is validated to detect altered records (11.10(a)); and records remain accurately and readily retrievable through retention (11.10(c), 211.180). The 'attributable/contemporaneous' (ALCOA) vocabulary comes from FDA data-integrity guidance.
system_implications: Engineering judgment derived from the cited rules. Use an event-sourced or append-only versioned record store for GMP data: each entry is an immutable event carrying user, device, UTC server timestamp, site time zone, reason for any change, and a content hash chained to the previous event. The 'current' batch record view is a projection of these events. Signatures reference the hash of the exact record version. A trusted time source (NTP stratum with drift monitoring) must be used, and time-sync failures are alarms. Clock drift on edge devices beyond a threshold blocks data capture. Store UTC and render site-local time with offset (important for multi-site and daylight-saving changes). Database administrators must not be able to alter GMP tables without detection (separation of DBA duties, database activity monitoring, hash verification). Scope notes: event sourcing, hash chaining, drift-based capture blocking and DBA activity monitoring are engineering choices that exceed the 'ordinary means' standard of 11.70 and the text of 11.10(e); a mandatory reason for change is guidance-derived. Keep them where risk justifies it, and document them as design decisions rather than regulatory requirements.
note: Corrected: 'inseparably linked' overstated 11.70, which requires protection against excision, copying or transfer by ordinary means; anchors made explicit and guidance vocabulary labelled.

requirement: Operations must take place in specifically defined areas of adequate size, using separate or defined areas, or other control systems, that prevent contamination and mixups during: receipt, identification, storage and withholding of components, containers, closures and labeling until the QCU has sampled, tested or examined and released them; holding of rejected materials pending disposition; storage of released materials; storage of in-process materials; manufacturing and processing; packaging and labeling; quarantine of drug products before release; storage of released drug products; and control and laboratory work. Buildings need space for orderly placement of equipment and materials, and material and product flows must be designed to prevent contamination and mixups.
system_implications: Room/area master data with a type (e.g., quarantine store, rejected cage, dispensing booth, compression suite, packaging hall, aseptic core) and the activities and material statuses allowed there. Each MBR step is bound to permitted area types, and execution is blocked in an area not approved for that step. Where the firm relies on 'other control systems' instead of physical segregation (e.g., electronic quarantine inside a shared warehouse), the status/location control must be validated as equally effective: quarantined or rejected stock cannot be picked, issued or dispensed, and physical labels show the same status as the system. Moves of materials, intermediates and finished product between locations are recorded with time and user.
verification_test: Execute a dispensing step from a terminal bound to a room not approved for dispensing -> blocked. Pick a quarantined lot stored in an electronically segregated shared location -> blocked. Move a rejected lot into a released-stock location type -> blocked and logged.

requirement: Ventilation must be adequate, and where appropriate for the operation there must be equipment giving adequate control of air pressure, microorganisms, dust, humidity and temperature. Air filtration (prefilters and particulate filters) is used where appropriate on air supplied to production areas; if air is recirculated, measures must control recirculation of production dust; and areas where air is contaminated during production need adequate exhaust or equivalent control systems.
system_implications: The MBR can state required room conditions per step (e.g., temperature and relative humidity ranges for moisture-sensitive granulation, compression or coating; pressure cascade and running dust extraction for potent or sensitizing compounds). At step start and during execution the eBMR reads room status or BMS/EMS values; if a limit is breached the step is blocked or a deviation is raised, per MBR rules, and the readings for the step window are attached to the batch record.
verification_test: Simulate relative humidity above the MBR limit before a humidity-sensitive step -> start blocked or deviation required per configuration. Simulate a pressure-cascade alarm during potent-compound dispensing -> deviation created and linked to the batch. The batch report shows the environmental readings for each conditioned step.

requirement: Penicillin must be manufactured, processed and packed in facilities, and with air-handling systems, completely separate from those used for other human drug products. If there is a reasonable possibility that a non-penicillin product was exposed to penicillin cross-contamination, that product must be tested for penicillin by the method incorporated by reference, and it may not be marketed if detectable levels are found.
system_implications: Product and material master data carry a penicillin flag; scheduling and batch-record issuance prevent penicillin products or components from being assigned to non-penicillin facilities, rooms or equipment, and vice versa. If an event creates a reasonable possibility of penicillin exposure (e.g., a spill in a shared warehouse or a misrouted material), QA can put the affected non-penicillin lots on hold, and the release gate then requires a penicillin test result showing none detected.
verification_test: Issue a batch record for a penicillin product in a non-penicillin facility -> blocked. Flag a non-penicillin lot as potentially exposed -> release blocked until a penicillin test result showing none detected is attached.

requirement: Buildings used to make, process, pack or hold drug products must be clean, sanitary, free of vermin (laboratory animals excepted) and in good repair, with trash and organic waste removed promptly and hygienically. Written, followed procedures must assign responsibility for sanitation and describe cleaning schedules, methods, equipment and materials in enough detail. Further written, followed procedures govern the use of suitable rodenticides, insecticides, fungicides, fumigants and cleaning or sanitizing agents so that equipment, materials and product are not contaminated; pesticides may be used only if registered and used under FIFRA. These procedures also apply to contractors and temporary staff.
system_implications: Room master data holds a cleaning/sanitation status and schedule (with cleaning agent lot and performer) and a maintenance/out-of-service status. The pre-start or line-clearance step checks that room cleaning is current and the room is not under maintenance; otherwise the step is blocked. Room cleaning by contractors or temporary staff uses the same electronic procedure and qualification checks as for employees, and cleaning agents are chosen from an approved list.
verification_test: Start a batch in a room whose scheduled cleaning is overdue -> blocked. Put a room into maintenance status -> no step can start there. A contractor without the cleaning-procedure qualification cannot sign a room-cleaning record.

requirement: Equipment surfaces that touch components, in-process materials or product must not react with, add to or absorb from them to a degree that moves the product's safety, identity, strength, quality or purity outside official or established requirements. Substances needed to run equipment, such as lubricants or coolants, must not contact components, containers, closures, in-process materials or product in a way that does so.
system_implications: Equipment master data carries a qualification status (including review of product-contact materials), and only qualified equipment can be selected for a step. Where equipment uses lubricants or coolants that could reach product, the approved grade is recorded in maintenance records, and a leak or contact event observed during a batch forces a deviation linked to that batch.
verification_test: Select equipment whose qualification is expired or pending -> blocked. Record a lubricant-leak event on a running step -> deviation created and batch flagged for QA review.

requirement: Detailed written, followed procedures must cover how components, containers and closures are received, identified, stored, handled, sampled, tested, and approved or rejected. Each container or group of containers of these materials must carry a distinctive code for every lot of every shipment received; the code is then used when recording the lot's disposition, and each lot's status (quarantined, approved or rejected) must be identified.
system_implications: At receipt the system assigns a unique receiving/control code per lot per shipment (two deliveries of the same supplier lot get different codes), prints container labels bearing that code and the status, and uses the code as the key in disposition, dispensing and genealogy records. Status on screen and on physical labels must match, so a status change triggers relabelling or label re-validation.
verification_test: Receive the same supplier lot in two shipments -> two distinct receiving codes. Change status to Approved -> the label and status display update and dispensing scans read the new status. Attempt a disposition without the receiving code -> not possible.

requirement: On arrival and before acceptance, each container or group of containers of components, containers and closures is visually examined for correct content labeling, container damage or broken seals, and contamination. The materials then stay in quarantine until tested or examined, as appropriate, and released, with storage meeting 211.80.
system_implications: The receiving transaction includes a mandatory visual examination per container group (labeling against the order and material master, damage, seal integrity, contamination) with the examiner's identity; failures route to rejection or QA assessment. Received lots default to Quarantine and cannot be allocated, picked or dispensed until QCU release. Examination results form part of the 211.184(b) record.
verification_test: Complete a receipt without the visual examination -> not possible. Record a broken seal -> lot routed to QA hold. Try to dispense a newly received lot -> blocked (Quarantine).

requirement: Representative samples must be taken from each shipment of each lot of components, containers and closures; the number of containers sampled and the amount taken per container are based on sound criteria such as statistics on variability, confidence and precision, the supplier's quality history, and the quantity needed for analysis and for 211.170 reserve samples. Sampling must: clean container exteriors where needed so the material is not contaminated; open, sample and reseal containers without contaminating their contents or other materials; use sterile equipment and aseptic technique when needed; not composite top, middle and bottom sub-samples when such stratified sampling is required; label sample containers so the material, lot, source container, sampling date and sampler can be determined; and mark sampled containers to show samples were removed.
system_implications: If sampling runs through the eBMR/WMS: the sampling plan (number of containers and quantity per material and supplier status) is master data; the system selects or confirms the containers to sample, prints sample labels showing material, lot, source container ID, date and sampler, marks the sampled containers electronically and on the label, and records the quantity taken (including reserve quantity for active ingredients). For sterile-product components the plan can require aseptic sampling (booth, sterile tools) and records it. Stratified sub-samples are labelled individually and cannot be merged in the system.
verification_test: Sample a lot -> labels carry all five identification elements and source containers show a sampled mark. Sample fewer containers than the plan requires -> blocked or deviation. Merge top/middle/bottom sub-samples where stratified sampling is required -> blocked.

requirement: Each component must get at least one identity test (a specific one where it exists) and be tested for conformity with its written purity, strength and quality specifications; instead of full in-house testing, a supplier's report of analysis may be accepted if the manufacturer runs at least one specific identity test and establishes, and re-checks at appropriate intervals, the reliability of the supplier's results. Containers and closures are tested against their written specifications, or a supplier's certificate of testing is accepted provided the manufacturer does at least a visual identification and periodically validates the supplier's results. Components are examined microscopically when appropriate; lots liable to filth, insect infestation or other extraneous adulterants are examined against specifications for them; and lots with potential for objectionable microbial contamination, given their use, are micro-tested before use. Lots meeting the specifications may be approved and released; others are rejected.
system_implications: The QCU release transaction for a component, container or closure lot requires, according to material master settings: an identity result (always for components), full-test or CoA-reliance results, and microbial, filth or microscopic results where flagged. CoA reliance is selectable only while the supplier/material pair has a current supplier-results validation status; when that lapses the material reverts to full testing. For injectables, components with objectionable-microbe risk (e.g., certain excipients and closures) carry mandatory microbial test flags as the firm defines them.
verification_test: Release a component lot on a CoA alone without an in-house identity test -> blocked. Let the supplier validation status lapse -> CoA-based release no longer offered. Release a container lot on a certificate with no visual identification record -> blocked.

requirement: Approved components, drug product containers and closures must be used in rotation so that the oldest approved stock goes first; temporary and appropriate departures from this are allowed.
system_implications: Dispensing and line-side issue propose the oldest approved lot first (by approval date, or by a documented equivalent such as earliest retest/expiry where the SOP justifies it). Choosing another lot requires a recorded reason, reportable so that departures can be shown to be temporary and appropriate.
verification_test: With two approved lots available, the system proposes the older one; picking the newer one requires a reason, which appears in a rotation-exception report.

requirement: Drug product containers and closures must not react with, add to or absorb from the drug to a degree that changes its safety, identity, strength, quality or purity beyond official or established requirements, and the container-closure system must adequately protect the product against foreseeable external factors during storage and use that could cause deterioration or contamination.
system_implications: These are design and qualification requirements; the eBMR enforces them by allowing only the container-closure components specified in the approved master record (item code and approved grade/supplier) to be issued and scanned at filling or packaging, with substitutions requiring change control. For injectables, the container-closure checks defined in the MBR (e.g., capping/crimp checks) are executed and recorded.
verification_test: Scan a closure item code not in the MBR bill of materials -> blocked. Try to approve an MBR whose container-closure components are not qualified in master data -> approval blocked.

requirement: Written, followed warehousing procedures must provide for holding drug products in quarantine until the QCU releases them, and for storing drug products under temperature, humidity and light conditions that keep their identity, strength, quality and purity unaffected.
system_implications: Finished lots are created in Quarantine status and become shippable only through the QCU disposition signature; any movement before release is flagged as under quarantine. Product master data holds storage conditions (from labeling and stability data); the eBMR records conditions for bulk, intermediate and finished-product holds within the batch (e.g., cold-chain holds for injectables, light protection) and links warehouse excursion events to affected lots so QA can assess them and, where needed, trigger re-evaluation or a 211.192 investigation.
verification_test: Try to ship a finished lot in Quarantine -> blocked in the integrated WMS/ERP. Inject a temperature excursion for a storage location -> the affected lots are listed and flagged for QA assessment.

requirement: Laboratory controls must include scientifically sound specifications, standards, sampling plans and test procedures, and must determine conformance: for each lot within each shipment of components, containers, closures and labeling (with written descriptions of sampling and testing, and retesting of materials that can deteriorate); for in-process materials; and for drug products. In every case the samples must be representative and properly identified. Sampling and testing plans for drug products must state the sampling method and how many units per batch are tested, and must be followed.
system_implications: Every sample drawn during eBMR execution (in-process, finished product, stability, reserve) is created from an MBR-defined sampling plan (point, method, number of units or quantity), receives a unique sample ID and label (product, lot, sampling point, date/time, sampler), and is sent to LIMS with that identity. The system checks the quantity or unit count against the plan, records any departure as a deviation, and prevents results from being attached to a sample from a different lot.
verification_test: Take fewer units than the plan specifies -> deviation required. LIMS receives the sample with the correct lot and sampling point. Attach a result to a sample from another lot -> rejected.

requirement: Instruments, apparatus, gauges and recording devices must be calibrated at suitable intervals under an established written program that gives specific directions, schedules, limits for accuracy and precision, and remedial action when those limits are not met; devices that do not meet their specifications must not be used. Complete records of this periodic calibration must be kept.
system_implications: Every measuring device used in eBMR steps (balances, pH meters, thermometers, pressure gauges, checkweighers, filter integrity testers, chart recorders) is in the instrument master with its calibration schedule, accuracy/precision limits and status, and use is blocked when calibration is overdue or failed. When an as-found calibration fails, the system lists every batch and step measured with that device since its last passing calibration so QA can carry out the remedial impact assessment, which is linked to the calibration record.
verification_test: Record a failed as-found calibration for a balance -> the system lists the affected batches since the last passing calibration and blocks the balance until it is recalibrated. Calibration records are retrievable from each batch that used the device.

requirement: Complete records must be kept of any modification of an established test method, giving the reason and data showing that the modified method is at least as accurate and reliable for the material tested; and complete records must show how laboratory reference standards, reagents and standard solutions were tested and standardized.
system_implications: For tests executed in the eBMR, the method is fixed by the MBR version; any modification goes through change control with justification and comparative data before the MBR can use it, and during execution a method cannot be altered ad hoc (only a documented deviation is possible). Reagents and standard solutions used in shop-floor tests (e.g., pH calibration buffers, titrants, reference standards) are scanned by lot, checked for expiry and standardization status, and recorded with the result.
verification_test: Run a test using an expired pH buffer lot -> blocked. Change a test-method parameter in an Effective MBR without change control -> not possible.

requirement: A written, followed stability program must assess product stability, and its results are used to set storage conditions and expiration dates. It includes statistically based sample sizes and test intervals, storage conditions for retained samples, reliable and specific methods, testing in the marketed container-closure system, and, for products reconstituted at dispensing, testing both as dispensed and after reconstitution. Enough batches must be tested to set an appropriate expiration date, with the data kept; accelerated data may support a tentative date only while full shelf-life studies continue until that date is confirmed or corrected. Complete records of all stability testing are kept.
system_implications: The eBMR records stability samples drawn from a batch (quantity, marketed container-closure, storage condition, study ID) as sampling events linked to the stability study in LIMS. Expiry dates used in a batch come only from product master data whose shelf life references approved stability data; a tentative, accelerated-data-based shelf life is flagged so batches made under it can be found if the date later changes.
verification_test: Enroll a batch in a stability study -> the sampling event, quantity and container-closure appear in the BPR and LIMS. Change shelf life in the product master without a stability-data reference -> blocked. Query all batches labelled under a tentative expiry -> correct set returned.

clause: 211.167(c) (211.167(b), ophthalmic ointments, is outside the tablets/injectables scope)
requirement: Each batch of a controlled-release dosage form must undergo appropriate laboratory testing showing it meets the specification for the release rate of each active ingredient, using written test procedures that are followed.
system_implications: Product master data flags modified/controlled-release products; for them the release gate requires an in-specification drug-release (dissolution) result for every active ingredient before QA can sign release.
verification_test: For an extended-release tablet lot with one active ingredient's release-rate result missing -> release blocked; with all results in specification -> release allowed.

requirement: For each lot in each shipment of each active ingredient, an appropriately identified, representative reserve sample must be kept, of at least twice the amount needed for all tests that determine whether it meets its specifications, excluding sterility and pyrogen tests. It is kept until 1 year past the expiry of the last drug product lot that contains that active ingredient; for radioactive products (other than nonradioactive reagent kits), 3 or 6 months after that expiry depending on whether the dating period is 30 days or less or longer; and for OTC products exempt from expiry dating, 3 years after distribution of the last lot containing it.
system_implications: At receipt or sampling of an active-ingredient lot the system requires a reserve-sample record (quantity checked against twice the specification test quantity from the test plan, excluding sterility/pyrogen tests; storage location). The reserve's retention end date is recalculated from genealogy as later finished lots use that API lot, and disposal before that date is blocked.
verification_test: Receive an API lot and try to complete sampling without a reserve sample of sufficient quantity -> blocked. Use the API lot in a new batch with a later expiry -> the reserve retention date moves out accordingly; disposal before it -> blocked.

requirement: For each lot or batch of drug product, an appropriately identified, representative reserve sample must be kept under conditions consistent with the labeling, in the same immediate container-closure system as the marketed product (or one with essentially the same characteristics), of at least twice the amount needed for all required tests except sterility and pyrogen tests. Except for radioactive products, reserve samples from representative lots chosen by acceptable statistical procedures are visually examined at least once a year for signs of deterioration, unless examination would compromise the sample; any deterioration is investigated under 211.192, and results are recorded with the product's other stability data. Retention is 1 year after the product's expiration date, with shorter periods for radioactive products and 3 years after distribution for OTC products exempt from expiry dating.
system_implications: The filling or packaging MBR contains a reserve-sample step: quantity computed as at least twice the release-test quantity (excluding sterility/pyrogen tests), taken in the marketed immediate container-closure, labelled and moved to a reserve location stored per labeling. Reserve units are included in yield and label reconciliation. The system schedules the annual visual examination for statistically selected lots, records results, opens an investigation on deterioration, and blocks disposal before the retention end date.
verification_test: Complete packaging without the reserve-sample step, or with less than the computed quantity -> blocked. The annual examination list is generated and a recorded deterioration opens an investigation. Dispose of a reserve before 1 year past expiry -> blocked.

requirement: Procedures must make sure the firm's responsible officials, if they are not personally involved or already aware, are told in writing about investigations under 211.198 (complaints), 211.204 (returns) or 211.208 (salvage), about recalls, about FDA inspection-observation reports, and about any FDA regulatory action relating to good manufacturing practice.
system_implications: Usually a QMS function. Where the eBMR hosts or links investigations, opening a complaint-, return- or salvage-related investigation, or linking a recall to a lot, triggers a written notification to the configured responsible officials with acknowledgement tracking, and the notification record is linked to the lots concerned.
verification_test: Open a return-related investigation for a lot -> the configured officials receive a notification, and the notification with its timestamp appears in the investigation record.

requirement: Returned drug products must be identified as returns and held. If the conditions under which they were held, stored or shipped before or during return, or the state of the product, container, carton or labeling, cast doubt on their safety, identity, strength, quality or purity, they must be destroyed unless examination, testing or other investigation shows they meet appropriate standards; reprocessing is allowed if the result meets appropriate standards, specifications and characteristics. Return records must show the product name and label potency of the dosage form, the lot (or control or batch) number, the reason for return, the quantity returned, the date of disposition and the final disposition. If the reason for return implicates associated batches, a 211.192 investigation is required. Holding, testing and reprocessing of returns follow written procedures.
system_implications: Returns are received against the original lot (genealogy link) into a Returned/Hold status that blocks redistribution. The return record captures the mandatory fields (product and label potency, lot, reason, quantity, disposition date, final disposition) plus evidence on storage and shipping conditions. Disposition is QCU-only: destroy, return to stock only with documented examination or test evidence, or reprocess through the reprocessing path (US-211-115). A reason code that implicates other batches forces a linked 211.192 investigation, and return data feed the annual product review.
verification_test: Receive a return without a reason -> not possible. Return a lot to saleable stock without examination or test evidence -> blocked. Choose a reason code flagged as batch-related -> an investigation is created and linked to the original batch record.

requirement: Drug products exposed to improper storage conditions (extreme temperature, humidity, smoke, fumes, pressure, age or radiation) because of natural disasters, fires, accidents or equipment failures must not be salvaged and put back on the market. Where it is unclear whether products were so exposed, salvaging is allowed only with laboratory test and assay evidence (including animal feeding studies where applicable) that the products meet all applicable identity, strength, quality and purity standards, and with evidence from inspection of the premises that the products and their packaging were not exposed to improper conditions; organoleptic examination counts only as supplementary evidence. Records including name, lot number and disposition are kept.
system_implications: QA can place all lots in an affected location or time window on a Salvage-Hold status (selected through location and genealogy queries), blocking distribution. Any 'salvage' disposition requires both linked laboratory evidence and a premises-inspection record; a disposition supported only by organoleptic checks is refused. Records capture product name, lot and disposition, and salvage events feed the annual review and responsible-official notification (211.180(e)-(f)).
verification_test: Place a warehouse zone on salvage hold -> all lots in it are blocked. Try to release a salvage-hold lot with only an organoleptic record -> blocked. With lab evidence and a premises-inspection record, QA can release and the record shows name, lot and disposition.

requirement: Electronic signatures, with their records, that meet Part 11 are treated as equivalent to full handwritten signatures, initials and other signings required by FDA regulations, unless a regulation effective on or after 20 August 1997 specifically excludes them; compliant electronic records may be used instead of paper unless paper is specifically required. A handwritten signature applied to an electronic record (e.g., a name or mark written with a stylus on a device that captures it) is a handwritten signature, not an electronic signature, and must still satisfy 11.50 and 11.70.
system_implications: Wherever Part 211 calls for a signature or initials (e.g., full handwritten signature on the master record in 211.186(a), sign or initial in 211.182, tester and reviewer initials or signature in 211.194(a)(7)-(8), dated approval signature on labeling specimens in 211.186(b)(8)), the eBMR uses a full Part 11 e-signature (11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300), not a lighter acknowledge click. If stylus/handwritten capture is offered, it must show printed name, date/time and meaning and be bound to the record. The URS should inventory every predicate-rule signature point and the signature type used for it.
verification_test: Review the signature-point inventory: every Part 211 signature or initials requirement maps to a Part 11-compliant signature event. Try to complete a 211.182 cleaning-log entry with a non-signature acknowledgement -> not possible.

requirement: Anyone using a closed system to create, modify, maintain or transmit electronic records must apply procedures and controls designed to protect the records' authenticity and integrity, their confidentiality where appropriate, and to ensure a signer cannot readily repudiate a signed record as not genuine; paragraphs (a) to (k) list the minimum controls.
system_implications: Beyond the (a)-(k) controls: decide which eBMR data need confidentiality (e.g., proprietary formulas, personal data of operators, health-related exclusion notes) and restrict read access by role and site, with encryption in transit and at rest as a design choice; support non-repudiation by keeping an evidence package per signature (identity-verification record, authentication event, signature manifestation, audit trail) so a signer cannot credibly deny it.
verification_test: A user without formula-view permission cannot read the MBR composition. For a sampled signature, the system produces the identity-verification record, authentication event and audit trail tying it to the signer.
